title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Why keys exist
A string that tells the server who you are




An API key is only a string that identifies your requests. Remember the lectures on AWS?
Identification: who is making the request, and are they allowed to ask this
Quotas: 1,000 requests a day per key, so one user cannot exhaust the service
Abuse prevention: a misbehaving key can be switched off without punishing everyone else
Free keys are still keys. “Free” describes the price, not how carefully you handle it
A leaked free key can exhaust your quota, and run up a big bill in your name
Most keys arrive within a minute of filling in a form with your email address





NASA’s signup form: https://api.nasa.gov

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Where keys go
The query string is easier to write, the header is safer to send



In the query string
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
    params={"api_key": "YOUR_KEY_HERE"},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.json()["title"])
Simple, and some APIs offer nothing else

In a header
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.github.com/user/repos",
    headers={"Authorization":
             "Bearer YOUR_KEY_HERE"},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.status_code)
Preferred whenever the API supports it





Headers win because URLs get logged. They land in server logs, browser history, proxy caches, and the Referer header sent to the next site. A key in a URL can be used to identify a user, a project, or a specific request

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Key hygiene
Four steps, the same ones your final project repository needs

You already ran this routine in Lecture 14, when you talked to a language model

Put the key in a file called .env, one NAME=value per line, no quotes, no spaces around the =


NASA_API_KEY=abc123def456


Add .env to your .gitignore before your first commit
Read it in Python with python-dotenv

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
key = os.getenv("NASA_API_KEY")

Commit a .env.example with the names and no values, so collaborators know what to create


Never hard-code a key in a notebook or script, and never paste one into a slide, a screenshot, or a chat message
Committed a key by accident? Revoke it immediately, then reissue. Deleting the file in the next commit does not help, because git log -p still shows it

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Why I’m so strict about this
text:
Why I’m so strict about this
39 million leaked secrets in one year




GitHub reported more than 39 million secrets leaked across the platform in 2024 alone
Bots scan public repositories constantly; exposure from careless commits happens in minutes
AWS keys are the most frequently leaked type
GitHub blocks pushes with known secret patterns via push protection, but only for recognised formats
Your checklist: .gitignore first, .env.example committed empty, git diff --cached before every commit
Revoke a leaked key immediately, then treat the old one as public forever





Source: GitHub Security Blog, The next evolution of GitHub Advanced Security (1 April 2025). Push protection: docs.github.com

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Worked example
NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day



Ask for one day’s picture, save the answer, then read the quota headers

import os, json, requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
key = os.getenv("NASA_API_KEY", "DEMO_KEY")

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
    params={"api_key": key, "date": "2026-08-05"},
    timeout=10,
)
r.raise_for_status()

with open("data/nasa_apod.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(r.json(), f, indent=2)

# How much quota is left
print(r.headers["X-RateLimit-Limit"],
      r.headers["X-RateLimit-Remaining"])
10 8




os.getenv(name, default) falls back to DEMO_KEY, so the code runs before anyone has a key
Sign up at https://api.nasa.gov, and the key arrives by email
The docs promise DEMO_KEY 30 requests per IP address per hour and 50 per day
This response says the limit is 10. The header is the truth, the documentation is the promise
Read the header on every run, because limits differ by service and change without notice


KeyError: 'X-RateLimit-Limit' means this API does not send the header. Use r.headers.get(...) when you are not sure

text:
The response
Saved JSON on disk, read again without a new request



Read the snapshot and print the two fields we need
import json

with open("data/nasa_apod.json") as f:
    apod = json.load(f)

print(apod["date"], "|", apod["title"])
print()
print(apod["explanation"][:400], "...")

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Servers send data in pages
Each response carries one page and the instructions to fetch the rest



Read the metadata element of the saved first page
import json

with open("data/wb_gdppc_2023_page1.json") as f:
    payload = json.load(f)

print(payload[0])

{'page': 1, 'pages': 3, 'per_page': 100,
 'total': 265, 'sourceid': '2',
 'lastupdated': '2026-07-13'}







One indicator across all countries and all years runs to tens of thousands of records
Sending that in one response would be slow for you and expensive for the server
The metadata block from last class holds the instructions. It is the first element of the two-element list
total records exist, split into pages pages of per_page records. This response is page page
lastupdated gives the date the World Bank last revised these numbers

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Reading the metadata block
Four fields decide how many requests you have to send




Field
Meaning
Why it matters




page
Which page this is
Your position in the loop


pages
How many pages exist
When to stop


per_page
Records per page
You can often raise this


total
Records in total
Sanity check at the end





Ask for a bigger page first. A request that needs 35 pages at per_page=500 needs one page at per_page=20000
The World Bank ceiling is per_page=32767. Ask for 32768 and the server answers 400, so 20000 is a safe value for one-page requests
Check the documentation for the ceiling of the API you are using. If the ceiling is too low, you loop

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Pattern 1: the page-number loop
Ask for page 1, read how many pages exist, repeat until the last one



Collect GDP per capita for 2023, 100 rows at a time

import requests, time

url = ("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all"
       "/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.KD")
records, page = [], 1

while True:
    params = {"format": "json", "date": 2023,
              "per_page": 100, "page": page}
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    meta, rows = r.json()

    records.extend(rows)
    print(f"page {meta['page']} of {meta['pages']}: "
          f"{len(rows)} rows")

    if page >= meta["pages"]:
        break
    page += 1
    time.sleep(0.5)          # be polite

print(f"collected {len(records)} records")
page 1 of 3: 100 rows
page 2 of 3: 100 rows
page 3 of 3: 65 rows
collected 265 records




The loop reads pages from the response instead of a hard-coded number, so it stays correct when countries are added
Use while True with a break, because pages does not exist until the first response arrives
The last page is short. 100 + 100 + 65 matches the total of 265
time.sleep(0.5) adds one and a half seconds in total





The same loop on total population: 35 pages, 17,490 records

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: The same loop, running on cached pages
text:
The same loop, running on cached pages
Three saved files replace the server, and the logic does not change



Open page 1, page 2, page 3 from disk instead of the network
import json

records, page = [], 1

while True:
    path = f"data/wb_gdppc_2023_page{page}.json"
    with open(path) as f:
        meta, rows = json.load(f)

    records.extend(rows)
    print(f"page {meta['page']} of {meta['pages']}: "
          f"{len(rows)} rows")

    if page >= meta["pages"]:
        break
    page += 1

print(f"\ncollected {len(records)} records "
      f"(metadata said {meta['total']})")
page 1 of 3: 100 rows
page 2 of 3: 100 rows
page 3 of 3: 65 rows

collected 265 records (metadata said 265)



Same structure and same stopping rule, with no network traffic
The three files came from the live loop on the previous slide
Comparing your record count with total is a cheap check that catches a dropped page
Testing a loop on saved pages costs the server nothing and runs instantly
Your project’s pull script will do exactly this: fetch once, then work from the files

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Pattern 2: cursor pagination
The server sends a token, and you return it with the next request




Not every API counts pages. Some return a token that points to the next batch
GitHub puts the next URL in a Link header. Follow it until rel="next" disappears
Others put a next_cursor or next_page_token in the body, and you send it in the next request
The logic is the same: fetch, collect, check whether more data exists, repeat
You lose the ability to plan. You cannot count the requests in advance or skip to page 7
You will not need this today. Recognise the pattern when you see it, then read the API documentation



GitHub’s Link header, from a real request

link: <https://api.github.com/repositories/
858127/issues?per_page=2&after=Y3Vyc29yOnYy
OpLPAAABoCyW3oD[...]&page=2>; rel="next"


The after= value is an opaque cursor, a bookmark that means something to GitHub and nothing to you
Send it back unchanged, and stop when the header no longer includes a next link

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Being a polite guest
Four habits that cost you nothing, and what to do about a 429




A loop can send hundreds of requests a second. A person with a browser cannot, and servers notice the difference


Sleep between requests. time.sleep(0.5) is invisible to you and helpful to the server
Read the documented limits and stay under them. Many APIs publish an exact number
Ask for bigger pages. One request for 20,000 rows is better than 200 requests for 100
Cache what you fetch so you never request the same data twice


When the header and the documentation disagree, trust the header, as the NASA example showed



A 429 often includes a Retry-After header with the waiting time

if r.status_code == 429:
    wait = r.headers.get("Retry-After", 60)
    print(f"rate limited, sleeping {wait}s")
    time.sleep(int(wait))


.get("Retry-After", 60) gives a fallback when the server sends no header
Without that header, use exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
Rapid retries against a struggling server turn a slowdown into an outage

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
pd.json_normalize: the flat case
Records with no nesting become a plain table



Pass three flat dictionaries and read the table back
import pandas as pd

flat = [
    {"code": "BRA", "year": 2023, "value": 76.4},
    {"code": "USA", "year": 2023, "value": 79.3},
    {"code": "JPN", "year": 2023, "value": 84.0},
]

print(pd.json_normalize(flat))
  code  year  value
0  BRA  2023   76.4
1  USA  2023   79.3
2  JPN  2023   84.0



Each dictionary key becomes a column, and each dictionary becomes a row
pd.DataFrame(flat) returns the same frame here, because there is nothing to flatten
The two differ as soon as a value is a dict or a list
pd.DataFrame keeps the dict in the cell. json_normalize expands it into columns
Missing keys become NaN in both, so uneven records do not raise an error

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
pd.json_normalize: the nested case
Nested dictionaries become columns named with a dot



Run it on the World Bank records from the previous slide
df = pd.json_normalize(records)

print(df.columns.tolist())
print()
print(df[["countryiso3code", "country.value",
          "date", "value"]].head(4).to_string(index=False))

['countryiso3code', 'date', 'value', 'unit',
 'obs_status', 'decimal', 'indicator.id',
 'indicator.value', 'country.id', 'country.value']

countryiso3code country.value date  value
            BRA        Brazil 2024 76.023
            BRA        Brazil 2023 75.848
            BRA        Brazil 2022 74.872
            BRA        Brazil 2021 73.038




Nested dictionaries became columns named with a dot: country.value, indicator.id
One nested level gives parent.child, two levels give parent.child.grandchild
Ten columns come from a record that looked like six fields
Use bracket notation, because df.country.value means something else to Python

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: When dots are not enough: record_path and meta
text:
When dots are not enough: record_path and meta
Dots flatten a dictionary. A nested list needs you to name the rows




Each item holds a list of observations, so name that list

payload_nested = [
    {"country": "Brazil", "iso3": "BRA",
     "observations": [{"year": 2022, "value": 76.0},
                      {"year": 2023, "value": 76.4}]},
    {"country": "Japan", "iso3": "JPN",
     "observations": [{"year": 2022, "value": 84.0},
                      {"year": 2023, "value": 84.1}]},
]

out = pd.json_normalize(
    payload_nested,
    record_path="observations",   # the list that becomes rows
    meta=["country", "iso3"],     # carried down onto each row
)
print(out.to_string(index=False))
 year  value country iso3
 2022   76.0  Brazil  BRA
 2023   76.4  Brazil  BRA
 2022   84.0   Japan  JPN
 2023   84.1   Japan  JPN



record_path names the list to explode into rows
meta names the parent fields to repeat on every row from that parent
Two parents holding two observations each give four rows
Without record_path you get two rows and a column of lists
The World Bank never needs this. Many other APIs do

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Cleaning the frame
A rectangle is not yet a tidy dataset



Build the four columns we need, with the correct dtypes
tidy = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": df["country.value"],
    "iso3": df["countryiso3code"],
    "year": df["date"].astype("int16"),
    "value": pd.to_numeric(df["value"],
                           errors="coerce"),
})

print(tidy.dtypes)
print()
print(tidy.head(3).to_string(index=False))
country        str
iso3           str
year         int16
value      float64
dtype: object

country iso3  year  value
 Brazil  BRA  2024 76.023
 Brazil  BRA  2023 75.848
 Brazil  BRA  2022 74.872



Rename the columns to plain words. country.value is the API’s vocabulary
Fix the dtypes. year and value arrive as strings (str), and a mean over strings fails or gives a wrong answer
errors="coerce" turns unreadable values into NaN instead of raising an error
Gaps are normal in international statistics, so keep them visible instead of stopping the script
Drop the columns you will not use. Six of the ten here repeat the same string



The project starter’s tidy() does the same flattening with a list comprehension and Polars. json_normalize is the pandas shortcut for this step. The project asks for Polars or DuckDB in the main work

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
One function: get_wdi
Decide what the function promises before writing the body



Write the signature and the docstring first, with no body
def get_wdi(indicator, countries="all",
            start=1990, end=2023):
    """Fetch one World Development Indicator
    as a tidy DataFrame.

    Parameters
    ----------
    indicator : str   WDI code, e.g. "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
    countries : str   "all", or ISO3 codes joined
                      by ";", e.g. "BRA;USA"
    start, end : int  First and last year, inclusive

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame with columns country, iso3, year,
    value (one row per country-year)
    """



So far we have written loose lines in a notebook, which is fine for learning
A project needs one name you can call twice and trust both times
The docstring makes you decide what the function does before you decide how
Defaults hold the choices you make most often, so most calls pass one argument
This is the most reusable part of the module, and you will copy it into your project

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
get_wdi, the body
Build the URL, then loop until the metadata says to stop



import time
import pandas as pd
import requests

def get_wdi(indicator, countries="all", start=1990, end=2023):
    """(docstring as on the previous slide)"""
    url = ("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/"
           f"{countries}/indicator/{indicator}")
    params = {"format": "json", "date": f"{start}:{end}",
              "per_page": 20000, "page": 1}

    records = []
    while True:
        r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=60)
        r.raise_for_status()
        payload = r.json()

        # An error comes back as a dict, not a two-element list
        if isinstance(payload, dict) or payload[1] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No data for {indicator}. "
                             "Has the code been retired?")

        meta, rows = payload
        records.extend(rows)

        if params["page"] >= meta["pages"]:
            break
        params["page"] += 1
        time.sleep(0.5)

    # the frame is built on the next slide



per_page=20000 usually fits the whole request into one page. The loop still runs when it does not
The World Bank ceiling is 32767, so 20000 leaves room and never causes a 400
payload[1] is None catches a valid two-element reply whose record list is empty
isinstance(payload, dict) catches the other error shape the API sends
records collects raw dictionaries across pages and stays unchanged until the loop ends
timeout=60 is generous, because a 20,000-row page takes a few seconds to build

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
get_wdi, the body (continued)
Flatten the records once, at the end, and return four named columns



The last four lines of the function
    df = pd.json_normalize(records)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "country": df["country.value"],
        "iso3": df["countryiso3code"],
        "year": df["date"].astype("int16"),
        "value": pd.to_numeric(df["value"],
                               errors="coerce"),
    }).sort_values(["country", "year"])
Call it like any other function
le = get_wdi("SP.DYN.LE00.IN", "BRA;USA", 2000, 2023)
print(le.head())



Flattening happens once, after every page arrives, instead of page by page
The four columns are the same ones we built by hand two slides ago
Sorting by country and year gives the caller a predictable order for plots and differences
The caller never sees pages, per_page, or a dotted column name
Every slide in this section contributed one line of this function

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Why the error check matters
The World Bank answers a retired indicator with 200 and an error message



Ask for a code that was removed and read the response
# EN.ATM.CO2E.PC was the CO2 per capita code
# for years. It is gone
r = requests.get(
    "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all"
    "/indicator/EN.ATM.CO2E.PC",
    params={"format": "json", "date": 2020},
)
print(r.status_code)
print(r.json())

200
[{'message': [{'id': '175',
   'key': 'Invalid format',
   'value': 'The indicator was not found. It may
have been deleted or archived.'}]}]




raise_for_status() sees a 200 and raises nothing
The parsing code then fails three lines later, with a confusing message
A successful HTTP request is not a successful data request
The isinstance(payload, dict) line turns that into one clear error message
EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5 replaced it, and this course uses that code


Indicator codes are retired without warning. Read the body of the response on every pull, and treat the status code as half the answer

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Caching: fetch once, read forever
Use the network the first time, then read from disk on every later run



Check the file before you call the server
from pathlib import Path

def get_wdi_cached(indicator, countries="all",
                   start=1990, end=2023):
    """get_wdi with a local cache."""
    cache = (Path("data") /
             f"{indicator}_{countries}_{start}_{end}.parquet")

    if cache.exists():
        print(f"reading {cache.name} from disk")
        return pd.read_parquet(cache)

    print(f"fetching {indicator} from the World Bank")
    df = get_wdi(indicator, countries, start, end)
    cache.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    df.to_parquet(cache, index=False)
    return df


Eight lines, four benefits

Speed: the second run is instant
Courtesy: you stop requesting data you already have
Reproducibility: your numbers stay the same while you write about them
Offline work: your analysis runs on a plane
scripts/pull_data.py in the project starter does the same, and saves the raw JSON next to the tidy table
These slides are built this way: every call was made once, saved to data/, and read back at render time

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
CSV or parquet?
One format a person can open, one format your code should read












CSV
Parquet




Format
Text, row-oriented
Binary, columnar, compressed


Dtypes
Loses them: int16 → int64, categories → strings
Keeps exactly what you saved


Column selection
Reads all columns, even if you need three
Reads only the columns you ask for


Size
Large (numbers stored as digit characters)
Typically 3-6x smaller


Ecosystem
Any tool, including spreadsheets
Needs pyarrow; pandas, Polars, DuckDB, R, Spark all read it


Human-readable
Open in any text editor
Needs code to read



df.to_parquet("data/wdi_panel.parquet", index=False)
df = pd.read_parquet("data/wdi_panel.parquet")




The format’s home page: https://parquet.apache.org




Rule of thumb: CSV for a person, parquet for everything your code reads
The project starter writes CSV and does not pin pyarrow, so parquet is optional there
If you use parquet in your project, add pyarrow to requirements.txt

Appendix 01
Exercise 01 solution

import requests, time

url = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL"
records, page = [], 1

while True:
    r = requests.get(url, params={"format": "json", "per_page": 500, "page": page}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    meta, rows = r.json()

    records.extend(rows)
    if page == 1:
        print(f"{meta['total']:,} records across {meta['pages']} pages")

    if page >= meta["pages"]:
        break
    page += 1
    time.sleep(0.5)

print(f"collected {len(records):,} records")
assert len(records) == meta["total"], "collected count does not match the metadata"
17,490 records across 35 pages
collected 17,490 records
Three things worth copying from this solution

The stopping rule reads meta["pages"], so the loop is still correct when the World Bank adds a country or a year
The assert at the end is a good habit
A pagination loop that drops a page without warning is a bug you notice only when your analysis is wrong

That run took 41 seconds: 35 requests, each followed by half a second of sleeping. With per_page=20000 the same data arrives in one call. The loop is the skill to learn, and a bigger page is the practical answer

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 04: the full get_wdi
The reference version, ready to copy

Copy this into your project
import time
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import requests


def get_wdi(indicator, countries="all", start=1990, end=2023):
    """Fetch one World Development Indicator as a tidy DataFrame.

    Parameters
    ----------
    indicator : str    WDI code, e.g. "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"
    countries : str    "all", or ISO3 codes joined by ";", e.g. "BRA;USA"
    start, end : int   First and last year, inclusive

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame with columns country, iso3, year, value
    """
    url = f"https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/{countries}/indicator/{indicator}"
    params = {"format": "json", "date": f"{start}:{end}", "per_page": 20000, "page": 1}

    records = []
    while True:
        r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=60)
        r.raise_for_status()
        payload = r.json()

        if isinstance(payload, dict) or payload[1] is None:
            raise ValueError(f"No data for {indicator}. Has the code been retired?")

        meta, rows = payload
        records.extend(rows)

        if params["page"] >= meta["pages"]:
            break
        params["page"] += 1
        time.sleep(0.5)

    df = pd.json_normalize(records)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "country": df["country.value"],
        "iso3": df["countryiso3code"],
        "year": df["date"].astype("int16"),
        "value": pd.to_numeric(df["value"], errors="coerce"),
    })

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 04: the caching wrapper
The second half of the reference version

Put this in the same file, below get_wdi
def get_wdi_cached(indicator, countries="all", start=1990, end=2023, cache_dir="data"):
    """Like get_wdi, with the network used once per set of arguments."""
    cache = Path(cache_dir) / f"{indicator}_{countries}_{start}_{end}.parquet"
    if cache.exists():
        return pd.read_parquet(cache)

    df = get_wdi(indicator, countries, start, end)
    cache.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    df.to_parquet(cache, index=False)
    return df
The cache filename includes every argument, so a new year range fetches a new file instead of returning the old one. Delete the file when you want fresh numbers

section: Module 06: getting data from the web
text:
Module 06: getting data from the web
What we did in lectures 18 and 19




A web API is a contract between your code and a server
We sent HTTP requests and read the JSON that came back
We handled pagination and wrapped the whole download in get_wdi()
Pages without an API need requests and BeautifulSoup instead
We saved every result as a parquet file, which keeps column types and compresses well
Today we ask what happens when those files get really big!



This module is called Scaling and Performance because “parallelise” is only one of the answers
Sometimes parallelism really is the right move
Sometimes the fix is a better algorithm
Sometimes we need a faster engine (next lecture)
We will cover all three strategies across these two lectures


Worth noticing: the parquet files we wrote in Module 06 are exactly the format Dask reads

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Lecture outline
What we will cover today




Serial vs parallel execution

map function and embarrassingly parallel problems

Big O notation and what parallelism can (and cannot) fix
Amdahl’s law: the speed-up ceiling
The GIL: why threads do not always help in Python
joblib and concurrent.futures for single-node parallelism

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Serial execution
One line finishes before the next one starts


A typical Python program runs its lines one after another, in order:


# Import packages
import numpy as np

# Define an array of numbers
foo = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

# Define a function that squares numbers
def bar(x):
    return x * x

# Loop over each element and perform an action on it
for element in foo:
    # Print the result of bar
    print(bar(element))

0
1
4
9
16
25

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The map function
Apply one function to every element of a list




We will use a tool called map later in this lecture
It applies one function to each element of a list or array
Here is a version I wrote by hand so you can see the loop inside it:



# (Very) inefficient function
def my_map(function, array):
    # create a container for the results
    output = []

    # loop over each element
    for element in array:
        
        # add the intermediate result
        output.append(function(element))
    
    # return the now-filled container
    return output





my_map(bar, foo)

[np.int64(0),
 np.int64(1),
 np.int64(4),
 np.int64(9),
 np.int64(16),
 np.int64(25)]




Python already provides a map function in its standard library, so you never have to write mine:



list(map(bar, foo))

[np.int64(0),
 np.int64(1),
 np.int64(4),
 np.int64(9),
 np.int64(16),
 np.int64(25)]




The built-in version returns the same answer and runs much faster than mine (it is implemented in C), so use it instead

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Using joblib for parallel computing
Two functions turn a loop into parallel work




Each step of our map call is independent, so nothing stops us running the steps at the same time
joblib gives us two functions for that
Parallel(n_jobs=k) runs k tasks at the same time
delayed(f) wraps f so that joblib can schedule the call instead of running it immediately
You combine them with a generator expression, as shown on the right
n_jobs=-1 asks joblib to use all available CPU cores
joblib handles process creation, data transfer and result collection for you
More details in the joblib documentation



Using our bar function and foo array from before:



# Install joblib if you haven't done so yet
# !pip install joblib

# Import joblib functions 
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

results = Parallel(n_jobs=6)(
    delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo
)
results

[np.int64(0),
 np.int64(1),
 np.int64(4),
 np.int64(9),
 np.int64(16),
 np.int64(25)]




joblib starts six workers and gives each one a different element of foo
The results match the serial version exactly, because the work itself has not changed

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Serial vs parallel execution
Four heavy calls, timed for real




calculation runs ten heavy operations on ten million random numbers
Each call is fully independent of the others, which makes this problem embarrassingly parallel
We time three things with %timeit: one call as a baseline, four calls in serial, and four calls in parallel
One call:



def calculation(size=10000000):
    # Create a large array and perform operations
    arr = np.random.rand(size)
    for _ in range(10):
        arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr)
    return np.mean(arr)

# Single run
%timeit calculation()

422 ms ± 11.3 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)





Four calls, serial:



# Sequential runs (4 times)
%timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)]

1.71 s ± 45.5 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)




Four calls, parallel:



%%timeit
# Parallel runs (4 times)
Parallel(n_jobs=4)(
    delayed(calculation)() for _ in range(4)
)

589 ms ± 10.8 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)




On my machine the parallel version does not reach a full 4× speed-up, because starting the workers and moving the results back costs time. The saving is still real

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
concurrent.futures: the standard-library option
The same pattern ships with Python itself




concurrent.futures comes with Python
A slow task is slow for one of two reasons: the processor is busy, or the processor is idle while your code waits for an answer
CPU-bound: the processor is busy with a task. Only more processors help, so use ProcessPoolExecutor, which works like joblib
I/O-bound: the processor is idle, waiting for a web server, a disk, or a database to answer. Use ThreadPoolExecutor
Both copy the map interface: a function and an iterable



from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(bar, foo))

results
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]




Waiting needs no second processor, so cheap threads do the job and no processes are spawned:



from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import requests

urls = [
    "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json",
    "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IND/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json",
    "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/USA/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json",
]

def fetch(url):
    return requests.get(url).json()

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
    results = list(executor.map(fetch, urls))



In lecture 19 you downloaded World Bank indicators one country at a time
This is the same get_wdi() pattern, with all three requests now running at the same time

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
When to use which?
sklearn and joblib




joblib suits numeric loops and scikit-learn. sklearn calls joblib internally whenever you set n_jobs=-1:



from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.svm import SVC
import time

digits = load_digits()
param_grid = {"C": [0.1, 1, 10], "gamma": [0.001, 0.01]}

start = time.time()
search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), param_grid, cv=3, n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(digits.data, digits.target)
elapsed = time.time() - start

print(f"Best score: {search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"Time: {elapsed:.2f}s (all cores)")

Best score: 0.976
Time: 2.59s (all cores)





concurrent.futures suits I/O parallelism, and anywhere you cannot install extra packages





Scenario
Tool




sklearn / numeric loops
joblib (n_jobs=-1)


Download many files
ThreadPoolExecutor


CPU-heavy, no dependencies
ProcessPoolExecutor


Bigger than RAM, clusters
Dask (next section)





Every tool does the same thing: split the work, run it on separate workers, then collect the results

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Big O notation
Runtime growth decides whether parallelism helps




Big O notation describes how the runtime grows as the input grows
O(1) means constant: reading one array element costs the same whatever the array size
O(n) means linear: a single loop takes twice as long when the input doubles
O(n²) means quadratic: a nested loop takes four times as long when the input doubles
Our calculation function called on n inputs is O(n)
Two calls take about twice as long as one, and a hundred calls take about a hundred times as long





Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Simulate processing times
num_images = np.array([1, 10, 50, 100, 200])
sequential_time = num_images * 2  # 2 seconds per image
parallel_time = (num_images * 2) / 4  # 4 cores, ideal speedup

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(num_images, sequential_time, 'o-', label='Serial O(n)', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
plt.plot(num_images, parallel_time, 's-', label='Parallel O(n/4)', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
plt.xlabel('Number of Images', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Time (seconds)', fontsize=12)
plt.title('O(n) Scaling: Serial vs Parallel', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.legend(fontsize=11)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What parallelism does to complexity




With p cores, an O(n) problem becomes O(n/p + overhead)
Four cores give you close to a 4× saving, minus whatever the coordination costs
The best candidates are embarrassingly parallel O(n) tasks
Running n independent calculations qualifies
Applying the same function to n separate inputs qualifies too
What both have in common is no shared state and no dependency between tasks


Parallelism never changes the Big O class. It divides the constant in front of it. An O(n²) algorithm running on eight cores is still an O(n²) algorithm; you only reach “too slow” a little later



A poor candidate for parallelism:



# O(n^2): every pair of elements
def pairwise_sum(data):
    n = len(data)
    results = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            results.append(data[i] + data[j])
    return results

data = list(range(1_000))
print(f"{len(pairwise_sum(data)):,} operations")

1,000,000 operations




A thousand elements already means a million operations
At n = 100_000 the same code is 10 billion operations, and no core count rescues that
Other poor candidates are steps that depend on previous results, algorithms with shared state, and problems limited by memory rather than by the CPU

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Try it yourself! 🧠


Install the packages with pip install joblib numpy if you have not done so already
Run the serial version below and write down the time it prints



def square(x):
    return x**2

# Create a large array to process
numbers = np.arange(1000000)

# Sequential version
%timeit [square(x) for x in numbers]



Now run the parallel version and write down its time as well. Be patient: this one takes a while

# Parallel version
%timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers)



Compare the two times and decide which version you would ship

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Amdahl’s law: the speed-up ceiling
The serial share caps the speed-up




Every program has a serial share: the setup, the merging of results, and any step that must wait for the one before it
Amdahl’s law says that share caps your maximum speed-up, however many cores you add
The formula is \(\text{speedup} = \dfrac{1}{s + \dfrac{p}{N}}\), where \(s\) is the serial fraction, \(p = 1 - s\) is the parallel fraction, and \(N\) is the number of cores
Take a program that is 90% parallel, so \(s = 0.1\), running on 8 cores
The arithmetic gives \(\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.9/8} = \frac{1}{0.2125} \approx 4.7\times\), well short of the \(8\times\) you might have hoped for





Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

cores = np.arange(1, 65)
serial_fracs = [0.05, 0.2, 0.5]
labels = ["5% serial", "20% serial", "50% serial"]
colours = ["#1B3A6B", "#E07A24", "#2CA02C"]

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
for s, lab, c in zip(serial_fracs, labels, colours):
    speedup = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / cores)
    plt.plot(cores, speedup, label=lab, linewidth=2, color=c)

plt.xlabel("Number of cores", fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Speed-up (×)", fontsize=12)
plt.title("Amdahl's law: speed-up vs core count",
          fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.legend(fontsize=11)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The GIL
Why threads do not always help in Python




CPython, the Python you are running, has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
The GIL lets only one thread execute Python code at a time, however many cores you have
Threads still help while your code waits, because the lock is released during downloads and API calls
They do nothing while your code computes, because the lock keeps the other threads idle
CPU-bound work needs processes: each process is a separate Python with its own GIL
NumPy, Polars and DuckDB release the GIL while their C and Rust code runs, so they use all cores with no processes to manage
A free-threaded build without the GIL is official since Python 3.14 (PEP 779), but it is not the default



How the GIL maps onto the tools you already know:










Task
Use
Why




Number crunching
Processes (joblib, ProcessPoolExecutor)
Sidesteps the GIL


Downloading many URLs
Threads (ThreadPoolExecutor)
GIL released while waiting


NumPy / Polars / DuckDB
Either or neither
Heavy work runs in C/Rust, outside the GIL


sklearn with n_jobs=-1
Processes (via joblib)
Each fold trains independently

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask
Familiar pandas code on data bigger than your RAM




Dask is a parallel computing library for Python
It scales the previous sections to datasets bigger than RAM and to clusters bigger than one machine
You write ordinary NumPy and pandas code; Dask handles the parallelism
Its task scheduler splits your work into a graph of small tasks and spreads them across your cores
Its big data collections are arrays, DataFrames and lists that behave like the ones you know
Active development, with a release most months: version 2026.8.0 was released in August 2026
Next lecture: when do you actually need Dask, and when does a faster single-machine engine win?





https://www.dask.org/


joblib parallelises your functions and leaves the data where it was. Dask chunks the data itself, so a Dask array or DataFrame can be larger than your RAM

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask arrays
NumPy arrays split into chunks that run in parallel




Let’s import Dask and see how it works



import dask.dataframe as dd
import dask.array as da



A Dask array is a parallel version of a NumPy array
It splits one large array into chunks, and every chunk is an ordinary NumPy array
Dask processes those chunks in parallel across your CPU cores
You choose the chunk size when you create the array, and here each block is 100 by 100
The API matches NumPy, so a.sum(), a.mean() and slicing all work as you expect



Let’s build a Dask array from a large NumPy array
The Dask array a is a lazy wrapper around the original data, split into 100 by 100 chunks



data = np.random.normal(size=100000).reshape(200, 500)
a = da.from_array(data, chunks=(100, 100))
a












Array
Chunk




Bytes
781.25 kiB
78.12 kiB


Shape
(200, 500)
(100, 100)


Dask graph
10 chunks in 1 graph layer

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask arrays
Nothing runs until you call .compute()


Dask arrays are lazy, so nothing is computed until you call .compute()
That lets you build a full computation graph, an execution plan, before any work starts
Dask can then optimise the graph and cut memory use before it executes anything
Let’s slice the Dask array a to get the first 10 rows of the sixth column



a[:10, 5] # first 10 rows of the 6th column












Array
Chunk




Bytes
80 B
80 B


Shape
(10,)
(10,)


Dask graph
1 chunks in 2 graph layers


Data type
float64 numpy.ndarray




         10 1








The .compute() method is what finally asks Dask for the numbers



a[:10, 5].compute()

array([-0.47002976,  2.05498662, -1.71513943, -1.48621739,  0.60905255,
       -3.212458  ,  2.42113634, -0.30261545,  2.05459781, -0.61635992])

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask arrays


Dask arrays support most of the NumPy operations you already use
Arithmetic works elementwise, so +, *, exp and log behave normally
Reductions along an axis work too, including sum(), mean() and std()



a.sum().compute()

np.float64(289.74681304463513)




Let’s time the same operation in NumPy on 100 million numbers



size = 100000000
np_arr = np.random.random(size)
%timeit np_result = np.sqrt(np_arr) + np.sin(np_arr)

550 ms ± 117 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)




And now the same operation in Dask, with the chunk size left to Dask



da_arr = da.random.random(size, chunks='auto')
%timeit (da.sqrt(da_arr) + da.sin(da_arr)).compute()

385 ms ± 25.8 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)




Not a rule: Dask wins here because sqrt and sin split cacross chunks. On data that fits in memory, building the graph and moving chunks often makes Dask slower. Run %timeit to see the difference

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask dataframes
Many pandas DataFrames behind one lazy interface




Dask also gives you a parallel version of the pandas DataFrame
One Dask DataFrame is many pandas DataFrames, split along the index
Let’s look at an example



import dask
df = dask.datasets.timeseries()

Why Parquet?
Column storage reads only what you ask for




CSV is row-based, so reading one column still means scanning every row
Parquet is column-based, so it reads the columns you named and skips the others




Feature
CSV
Parquet




Storage
Row-based
Column-based

None

182 MB

import pandas as pd

# CSV: reads everything, infers types
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")

# Parquet: reads only what you need
df = pd.read_parquet("sales.parquet",
                     columns=["date", "revenue"])


CSV is not obsolete: reach for parquet when you have many columns and query only a few, or when the file passes 100 MB. Stay with CSV for small files, one-off exports, and anything a collaborator will open in Excel

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask delayed
A decorator schedules any function you already have




Sometimes you do not want a whole Dask DataFrame or Dask array
You want to parallelise one function, or one small part of a script
dask.delayed does exactly that, and it works on functions you have already written
Here are four serial calls to a deliberately heavy function



def calculation(size=10000000):
    arr = np.random.rand(size)
    for _ in range(10):
        arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr)
    return np.mean(arr)

%timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)]

1.39 s ± 36.7 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)





The only change is the @dask.delayed decorator above the function



@dask.delayed
def delayed_calculation(size=10000000):
    arr = np.random.rand(size)
    for _ in range(10):
        arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr)
    return np.mean(arr)

results = []
for _ in range(4):
    results.append(delayed_calculation())

# Compute all results at once
%timeit final_results = dask.compute(*results)

611 ms ± 25.6 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)




Nothing in the body of the function changed
Calling delayed_calculation() builds a task instead of running one, so dask.compute(*results) is what triggers the work

Watching the task stream at localhost:8787




Starting a dask.distributed.Client() opens a diagnostics dashboard on port 8787
The task stream on the right is the same three-stage pipeline, run in a loop so the picture fills up
Each row is one worker thread, and each coloured bar is one task it ran
The three colours are generate_data, transform_data and aggregate_data

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Best practices
Cheaper fixes to try before you parallelise




Measure first: %timeit and cProfile will tell you where the time goes, and Amdahl’s law tells you what that share is worth
Ask two questions: are the tasks independent of each other, and is each one heavy enough to pay for starting a worker? If either answer is no, do not parallelise
Pick the right algorithm: an \(O(n \log n)\) solution beats a parallelised \(O(n^2)\) one on any interesting input
Pick the right engine: Polars or DuckDB may finish the job faster than a parallelised pandas, as we will see next lecture
Start small: NumPy or pandas may already have a fast function for what you wrote by hand
Sample first: ask whether the question really needs all of those terabytes



Switch to parquet: the format change alone bought us a large speed-up a few slides ago
Call .compute() and .persist() sparingly: every call triggers execution, so batch the work into one
Experiment with chunk sizes: try a few by hand, or start from chunks='auto'
The Dask team keeps a longer list at Dask best practices


The mistake I see most often: students parallelise before they profile. Run %timeit first. If the hot spot turns out to be disk reads or an \(O(n^2)\) loop, more cores will not save you, and you will have spent an afternoon finding that out

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What we learned today




Serial and parallel execution: map, embarrassingly parallel problems, and joblib for the easy cases
concurrent.futures ships with Python: ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU work, ThreadPoolExecutor for waiting
Big O notation: parallelism cuts the constant factor and leaves the complexity class alone
Amdahl’s law: the serial share caps your speed-up, so measure it before you buy cores
The GIL: threads help while Python waits, processes help while Python computes, and NumPy sidesteps both



Dask gives you lazy arrays and DataFrames for data bigger than RAM
dask.delayed parallelises functions you have already written, and dask.visualize shows the plan
Parquet cut our January 2000 data from 182 MB to 86 MB and made the group-by much faster
Next lecture, Scaling Data Analysis in Practice, puts Polars and DuckDB against pandas and Dask on the WDI panel. They use every core by default, with nothing to configure

Solution to the joblib exercise


Here is the solution to the exercise


def square(x):
    return x**2

# Create a large array to process
numbers = np.arange(1000000)

# Sequential version
%timeit [square(x) for x in numbers]

44.8 ms ± 475 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)



from joblib import Parallel, delayed

# Parallel version
%timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers)

Expected result: the parallel version is slower here. square(x) finishes so fast that joblib’s process-spawning overhead swamps the work. Parallel computing pays off when each task is heavy

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Parallel computing fundamentals
Where lecture 21 left us




Last class we covered the concepts of parallel and scalable computing:

map, embarrassingly parallel problems, and joblib / concurrent.futures
Big O: parallelism cuts the constant while the complexity class stays the same
Amdahl’s law: speed-up is capped by the serial share, so measure before scaling
The GIL: threads help for I/O, processes for CPU, and C/Rust libraries sidestep it entirely
Dask basics: lazy arrays and DataFrames for bigger-than-RAM data




We ended with a promise: some engines parallelise for you, with no cluster to manage
Today is the practice session: we decide which tool you actually reach for
We will meet Polars and DuckDB, then race all four engines on the WDI panel we built in Module 06

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Lecture outline
What we will cover today




Set up local Dask Clusters with workers, schedulers, and the dashboard
The single-machine renaissance: why most “big data” now fits on one laptop
Polars: a fast DataFrame library with lazy evaluation and streaming
DuckDB: SQL as an out-of-core scaling tool
The benchmark: pandas vs Polars vs DuckDB vs Dask on 200 million rows
Which tool when: a decision framework, plus a short word on GPUs







Every output on these slides comes from a real run on my laptop. The benchmark was measured once and saved to data/benchmark_results.csv

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What is a Dask Cluster?
Workers and schedulers


A Dask Cluster is a group of computational engines (cores, GPUs, servers, etc.) that work together to solve a problem
Workers provide two functions:

Compute tasks as directed by the scheduler. The scheduler is the brain of the cluster
Store and serve computed results to other workers or clients

Workers are the reason why lazy evaluation speeds up computations
Here is a simple example:


Scheduler -> Eve: Compute a <- multiply(3, 5)!
Eve -> Scheduler: I've computed a and am holding on to it! 
Scheduler -> Frank: Compute b <- add(a, 7)!
Frank: You will need a. Eve has a.
Frank -> Eve: Please send me a.
Eve -> Frank: Sure. a is 15!
Frank -> Scheduler: I've computed b and am holding on to it!

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What is a Dask Cluster?
How the scheduler assigns work


How do workers know what to do?

The scheduler assigns tasks to workers based on their availability
Workers can be on the same machine or on different machines
Workers can be CPUs or GPUs

These processes can automatically restart and scale up without any intervention from the user
The optimal number of workers depends on data size and computation complexity
The default configuration is usually enough
In an adaptive cluster, you set the minimum and maximum number of workers
The cluster adds and removes workers as the work demands
Dask also provides a dashboard to monitor the performance of your cluster

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Setting up a Dask Cluster
Installing the distributed scheduler


First, we need to install Dask and the distributed scheduler. I tested this with dask==2026.7.1 and distributed==2026.7.1


python -m pip install "dask==2026.7.1" "distributed==2026.7.1"


The distributed scheduler is the default for Dask and it works great 👍
Conda users can install it with:


conda install dask=2026.7.1 distributed=2026.7.1 -c conda-forge

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Setting up a Dask Client
One client at the top of your script


Using dask.distributed requires that you set up a Client
This should be the first thing you do if you intend to use dask.distributed in your analysis
It offers low latency, data sharing between the workers, and is easy to set up



from dask.distributed import LocalCluster, Client

# Specify a different port for the dashboard
# Use fewer workers and threads to avoid resource issues
cluster = LocalCluster(dashboard_address=':8789', n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=2)
client = Client(cluster)

# Print the dashboard link
print(f"Dask dashboard is available at: {cluster.dashboard_link}")

Dask dashboard is available at: http://127.0.0.1:8789/status




The Client object provides a way to interact with the cluster, submit tasks, and monitor the progress of computations
Opening that link in your browser gives you the dashboard on the next slide

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The Dask dashboard
The status page and the workers tab







The status page: bytes stored, task processing, and the task stream, all updating live while the cluster works






The workers tab: one row per worker, with its CPU, memory, and the number of tasks it is holding



Keep this open in a second window while you work. It is the fastest way to see whether the cluster is busy, idle, or running out of memory

# Perform a simple computation

# Compute the result

If the client misbehaves, Appendix 03 lists the errors you are most likely to hit






The task stream while y.compute() runs: every coloured bar is one chunk of the array being added and summed





The same run seen per worker: both workers stay busy, which is what parallel execution looks like

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
A reality check
“Big data” doesn’t only mean “buy a cluster”




For a decade, “big data” meant “buy a cluster”, and that assumption is now often wrong
A modern laptop has 8-16 cores and fast SSD storage
Most datasets that feel large (a few GB, tens of millions of rows) fit comfortably on one machine if the engine is written for it
Why does this matter for you?

No cluster to set up, pay for, or debug
Ordinary code, running fast
Enough for the final project and most real jobs

The old advice (“just use Spark”) often makes things slower at this size, because cluster coordination has real overhead
Two public benchmarks agree: Polars and DuckDB perform really well






Groupby on 5 GB, 16 cores and 32 GB RAM. DuckDB is one of the winners, and Polars does a great job too. Source: db-benchmark

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Why single-machine engines got so fast
text:
Why single-machine engines got so fast
The design decisions Polars and DuckDB share




Columnar memory (Apache Arrow): data is stored column by column, so a query reads only the columns it needs, streaming through contiguous memory
Vectorised kernels: the heavy loops are written in Rust (Polars) or C++ (DuckDB), running in batches on your CPU’s SIMD instructions
All cores by default: every query is parallelised across your cores, with no cluster and no n_jobs to set














“Average one column” then reads a tiny slice of the file






Source: pola.rs/posts/benchmarks

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What is Polars?
The product page, before the syntax




Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust
Its own headline is “DataFrames for the new era”
The numbers on the front page: 775 million downloads and 39,000 GitHub stars, under an MIT licence
It feels like pandas, with four differences:

The multi-threaded Rust engine uses all your CPU cores automatically
Data sits in Arrow columnar memory
A lazy mode optimises your whole query before running it
It can stream data larger than RAM

Install it with pip install polars






Source: pola.rs

# pandas
df.groupby("indicator").agg(
    mean_value=("value", "mean"),
    n=("value", "size"),
).head(3)


.alias("decade") names the new column
Polars never mutates in place; each step returns a new frame
Inside .agg() you list one expression per output column
pl.len() counts rows in each group

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Lazy mode: let the engine plan the query
text:
Lazy mode: let the engine plan the query
Nothing runs until you call collect




scan_parquet returns a lazy frame: nothing runs until you call .collect()
This lets Polars reorder and prune your query like a database would



lazy = (
    pl.scan_parquet("../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("year") >= 1990)
    .group_by("indicator")
    .agg(pl.col("value").mean())
)
result = lazy.collect()
result.head(3)


shape: (3, 2)



indicator
value


cat
f64




"primary_enrolment_net"
87.585799


"gdp_per_capita"
14330.646062


"urban_pop_pct"
57.766502









.explain() shows the optimised plan:



print(lazy.explain())

AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
  [col("value").mean()] BY [col("indicator")]
  FROM
  simple π 2/2 ["indicator", "value"]
    Parquet SCAN [../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet]
    PROJECT 3/5 COLUMNS
    SELECTION: col("year") >= 1990
    ESTIMATED ROWS: 59024




Read the nodes bottom-up: Polars pushes the filter and the column selection down into the file scan, so it never reads data it will throw away

It’s like mean(filter(read(file))): the outermost call is written first but happens last

π is projection (keep these columns) and SELECTION is the row filter, two ideas from relational algebra
Polars reads 3 of the 5 columns and drops the old rows before any data reaches your query

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Streaming: data larger than RAM
One argument changes how the query runs




The same lazy query can run in streaming mode
Polars processes the data in small batches, so the full dataset never sits in memory at once



result = (
    pl.scan_parquet("../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("year") >= 1990)
    .group_by("indicator")
    .agg(pl.col("value").mean())
    .collect(engine="streaming")
)
result.shape

(8, 2)





The only change is collect(engine="streaming")
This is how Polars handles files bigger than your RAM on a single machine
We use exactly this in the benchmark, on a file of 200 million rows


Note: the streaming engine has changed name across Polars versions. On Polars 1.43 (this deck) it is collect(engine="streaming")

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Polars and pandas can work together!
text:
Polars and pandas can work together!
Converting in both directions




You do not have to choose one forever
Convert in either direction:



# Polars -> pandas
pdf = result.to_pandas()

# pandas -> Polars
back = pl.from_pandas(pdf)
type(pdf), type(back)

(pandas.DataFrame, polars.dataframe.frame.DataFrame)





Typical pattern:

Do the heavy data work in Polars (fast, parallel)
Convert to pandas when a tool needs pandas: plotting with matplotlib, or feeding scikit-learn

The conversion is cheap because both use Arrow underneath

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
SQL as a scaling tool
The DuckDB home page, before the syntax




DuckDB is an in-process analytical database written in C++, and its own tagline is “Your universal data wrangling tool”
Think “SQLite for analytics”: no server, just pip install duckdb
Like Polars, it is parallel and out-of-core (it can process data larger than RAM)
Its trick: query files directly, with no loading step





Source: duckdb.org



Query a Parquet file straight from disk:



import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT indicator, AVG(value) AS mean_value
    FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet'
    WHERE year >= 1990
    GROUP BY indicator
    LIMIT 3
""")

┌────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│   indicator    │     mean_value     │
│    varchar     │       double       │
├────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ urban_pop_pct  │ 57.766502068009025 │
│ co2_per_capita │   4.87445669671352 │
│ population     │ 30804601.116427217 │
└────────────────┴────────────────────┘




The file path goes straight in the FROM clause. DuckDB reads only the columns and rows it needs

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Querying a DataFrame by name
Your Python variable becomes a SQL table




DuckDB can also query a DataFrame that already sits in a Python variable
The variable name becomes the table name in your SQL



import pandas as pd

pdf = pd.read_parquet(
    "../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet"
)

# The variable `pdf` is now a SQL table
duckdb.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM pdf")

┌───────┐
│   n   │
│ int64 │
├───────┤
│ 59024 │
└───────┘





Full SQL works: GROUP BY, joins, subqueries, window functions
country is a pandas category, which DuckDB reads as an enum: ::VARCHAR turns it back into plain text so the result prints tidily



duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country::VARCHAR AS country,
           ROUND(AVG(value), 1) AS mean_value,
           COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM pdf
    WHERE year >= 2000
    GROUP BY country
    ORDER BY mean_value DESC
    LIMIT 3
""")

┌───────────────┬─────────────┬───────┐
│    country    │ mean_value  │   n   │
│    varchar    │   double    │ int64 │
├───────────────┼─────────────┼───────┤
│ China         │ 192742978.9 │   192 │
│ India         │ 169301998.4 │   192 │
│ United States │  42274028.5 │   192 │
└───────────────┴─────────────┴───────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
When to use SQL
Choosing between expressions and SQL




Polars and DuckDB solve the same problems at similar speed
The choice is mostly about what you find readable:

Polars: method chains, expressions, feels like Python
DuckDB: SQL, familiar to anyone who took DATASCI 151

Many people use both: SQL for the big aggregation, Polars or pandas for the follow-up
A DuckDB result converts to either DataFrame with one method:

.df() gives a pandas DataFrame
.pl() gives a Polars DataFrame

So you can write the heavy query in SQL and continue in whichever library you prefer
The same hand-off pattern we saw with Polars




q = """
    SELECT indicator, AVG(value) AS mean_value
    FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet'
    WHERE year >= 1990
    GROUP BY indicator
"""

# To pandas
pdf = duckdb.sql(q).df()

# To Polars
pol = duckdb.sql(q).pl()

type(pdf), type(pol)

(pandas.DataFrame, polars.dataframe.frame.DataFrame)




Want more SQL practice? The course website has a full self-study DuckDB SQL tutorial. It covers SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, joins, and window functions with DuckDB, for anyone who skipped DATASCI 151 or wants more depth

text:
The four queries, side by side
Polars and DuckDB here; pandas and Dask in Appendix 05

Polars (lazy + streaming):

import polars as pl
(pl.scan_parquet("data/wdi_big.parquet")
   .filter(pl.col("year") >= 1990)
   .with_columns(((pl.col("year") // 10) * 10).alias("decade"))

           AVG(value) AS mean_value

Reading the benchmark honestly




Every benchmark measures one task on one machine
Treat the numbers as evidence about this setting, and expect them to shift with:

the task (this one is a simple aggregation)
the hardware (cores, RAM, disk speed)
the data shape and file layout

What stays the same:

The order of magnitude: Polars and DuckDB are far ahead for single-node analytics
The zero setup cost: no cluster, no config

The order of magnitude is the result worth remembering; the exact seconds will differ on your machine






The Dask task stream during the benchmark

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
A decision framework
What we have been building









Your situation
Reach for




Fits in RAM, quick exploration, plotting
pandas


Big single file or many files, one machine
Polars or DuckDB (expressions or SQL, your preference)


Bigger than the machine, a real cluster, or task graphs / arrays
Dask (or Spark in industry)



pandas → Polars/DuckDB → Dask




When Dask still wins:

Data larger than one machine’s disk
A real cluster of many machines
Parallel arrays and custom task graphs (the dask.delayed pipelines from last lecture)

Fast single-machine engines shrink the set of problems that need Dask. The cases above remain genuinely distributed



pandas is still the right default for small data and for the huge ecosystem around it
Polars and DuckDB answer “my data got big and still fits on one machine”
From last lecture, before you scale anything:

Amdahl first: measure where the time goes
A better algorithm or a faster engine often beats adding cores

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
A word on GPUs
When different hardware is worth the trouble




Everything today used your CPU, which are general-purpose processors with a few fast cores
A GPU has thousands of small, slow cores
That suits data-parallel work

The same operation applied to millions of numbers at once, like matrix multiplication

This is exactly what training a neural network needs
GPUs pay off when the work is the same arithmetic repeated across millions of values
Ordinary data wrangling rarely has that shape, which is why everything else today ran on the CPU



For data analysis, the GPU stack is RAPIDS, renamed CUDA-X in August 2026:

cuDF: DataFrames on the GPU
cuML: the same offer for scikit-learn






Source: NVIDIA CUDA-X

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
GPUs without rewriting your code




cudf.pandas accelerates pandas from one line

%load_ext cudf.pandas in a notebook

It covers the whole pandas API and falls back to the CPU, so your code still runs
The Polars GPU engine does the same for lazy Polars

You pass an engine to collect, and unsupported queries fall back to the CPU

It is still open beta, and NVIDIA aims it at datasets of hundreds of gigabytes and up
No GPU on your laptop? Google Colab gives you one for free, and both projects ship a Colab demo
Nothing in the final project needs a GPU

Measure where the time goes before you scale anything

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 03: When something goes wrong



No buffer space available
The cluster ran out of network resources for worker-to-worker traffic. Use a smaller array, or lower n_workers and threads_per_worker.
Stream is closed or CommClosedError
A worker died mid-computation, usually in an interactive terminal. Run the same code from a script or a Jupyter notebook instead.
The dashboard will not open
The port is already taken. Pick a free one with dashboard_address=':8789', or let Dask choose automatically.

Workers keep restarting
This is memory pressure. Lower n_workers, raise the memory limit, or process the data in smaller chunks.
The computation hangs
You probably created two clients. Restart the kernel and create exactly one Client

General advice: create one Client at the top of your script and reuse it. Watch the task stream and worker memory panels on the dashboard, and when in doubt restart the client and run on a smaller sample first

Parallel computing fundamentals
Where lecture 21 left us




Last class we covered parallel and scalable computing:

map, embarrassingly parallel problems, joblib and concurrent.futures
Big O: parallelism cuts the constant, the complexity class stays the same
Amdahl’s law: the serial share caps your speed-up, so measure before scaling
The GIL: threads for I/O, processes for CPU, C/Rust libraries sidestep it
Dask: lazy arrays and DataFrames for bigger-than-RAM data




We ended with a promise: some engines parallelise for you, with no cluster to manage
DuckDB is one of them, and today we use it to revise SQL
In Lecture 02 you voted for a SQL revision over a Polars class
All queries today run on the WDI panel you built in Module 06

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Lecture overview
What we will cover today



1. Why SQL and why DuckDB

A declarative language every engine speaks
import duckdb is the whole setup

2. First queries

SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, and the order a query really runs in

3. Aggregating

COUNT, AVG, GROUP BY, HAVING
What COUNT does when values are missing


4. NULLs, CASE and windows

IS NULL, COALESCE, income bands with CASE
A window function beside a GROUP BY

5. Joins

Primary keys, foreign keys, and the ON clause
INNER, LEFT, FULL OUTER on two tiny tables

6. SQL in Python

Querying a pandas DataFrame by its variable name
The same queries in plain sqlite3, which assignment 09 uses
DuckDB on 200 million rows

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Why SQL
You describe the answer, the engine finds it




SQL is a language for asking questions of tables
It is declarative: you say what you want, and the engine decides how to compute it

No loops, no index lookups, no merge strategy
The engine can reorder the query, read fewer columns, or use every core

SQL is about fifty years old, and data job adverts list it more often than any Python library
Dialects differ in the details, but SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and JOIN are the same in DuckDB, SQLite, PostgreSQL, BigQuery and Snowflake





DuckDB’s SQL introduction: https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/introduction

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Why DuckDB for a revision class
text:
Why DuckDB for a revision class
An in-process engine with no setup




Zero setup: pip install duckdb, then import duckdb. No server, no password
In-process: the database runs inside your Python session, like SQLite (“SQLite for analytics”)
Reads files by name: a Parquet or CSV path goes straight in the FROM clause
Reads a pandas DataFrame by its variable name too (more on this later)
Columnar and parallel underneath, so the same GROUP BY works on 200 million rows
Version on my laptop: DuckDB 1.5.5





Source: https://duckdb.org



Assignment 09 uses sqlite3 from the standard library. The sqlite3 section runs the same queries there, so nothing today is DuckDB-only

Querying a Parquet file
The file path goes in the FROM clause




The WDI panel: 59,024 rows of country, indicator, year and value
duckdb.sql() takes a query string and returns a result you can print
The path goes in single quotes: single quotes mean text, double quotes mean a column name
No read_parquet, no connection, no cursor
The column types under the names come from the Parquet file




import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT *
    FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet'
    LIMIT 5
""")

│ varchar │ varchar │    varchar     │ int16 │      double      │

│ Aruba   │ ABW     │ co2_per_capita │  1990 │ 3.20303411789078 │
│ Aruba   │ ABW     │ co2_per_capita │  1991 │ 3.43571688721622 │
│ Aruba   │ ABW     │ co2_per_capita │  1992 │  3.6345192377364 │

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Creating a view
One name for the file




A view is a saved query that behaves like a table

Ours is called wdi, so every later query says FROM wdi instead of the file path
It holds no data: DuckDB re-reads the Parquet file each time
OR REPLACE makes the cell safe to re-run

DESCRIBE lists the columns and their types
SUMMARIZE shows min, max, count and the share of missing values per column
11.06% of value is missing (more on this in the NULLs section)




duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW wdi AS
    SELECT * FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet'
""")

duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows,
           COUNT(DISTINCT country) AS countries,
           COUNT(DISTINCT indicator) AS indicators
    FROM wdi
""")

│  59024 │       217 │          8 │
└────────┴───────────┴────────────┘

    SELECT column_name, min, max, null_percentage
    FROM (SUMMARIZE SELECT country, year, value FROM wdi)
""")

│   varchar   │   varchar   │   varchar    │  decimal(9,2)   │

SELECT, aliases, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Picking columns and sorting the result




SELECT lists the columns you want (* means all of them)
AS renames a column in the output. The new name is an alias
SELECT can also compute, e.g. ROUND(value, 0)
ORDER BY value DESC sorts high to low (ASC is the default)
LIMIT caps the rows returned. Use it while exploring
Monaco, at 161,263 dollars per person, is the panel’s maximum




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, year,
           ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita'
      AND year = 2020
    ORDER BY value DESC
    LIMIT 5
""")
