│   country   │ year  │  gdp_pc  │
│   varchar   │ int16 │  double  │
├─────────────┼───────┼──────────┤
│ Monaco      │  2020 │ 161263.0 │
│ Luxembourg  │  2020 │ 105274.0 │
│ Bermuda     │  2020 │  98846.0 │
│ Isle of Man │  2020 │  86595.0 │
│ Switzerland │  2020 │  86294.0 │
└─────────────┴───────┴──────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: WHERE with AND, OR and NOT
text:
WHERE with AND, OR and NOT
Filtering rows with WHERE




WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true
AND requires both sides, OR requires either, NOT flips a condition
The brackets around the OR matter: AND binds tighter
Text goes in single quotes, and comparisons are case-sensitive in DuckDB
Without the NOT, Japan would fill the list
All five rows are from 2020, although we asked for 2000 too: life expectancy rose almost everywhere




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, year,
           ROUND(value, 1) AS life_exp
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'life_expectancy'
      AND (year = 2000 OR year = 2020)
      AND NOT country = 'Japan'
    ORDER BY value DESC
    LIMIT 5
""")

┌──────────────────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│       country        │ year  │ life_exp │
│       varchar        │ int16 │  double  │
├──────────────────────┼───────┼──────────┤
│ Monaco               │  2020 │     86.1 │
│ Hong Kong SAR, China │  2020 │     85.5 │
│ Macao SAR, China     │  2020 │     84.1 │
│ Singapore            │  2020 │     83.5 │
│ Korea, Rep.          │  2020 │     83.4 │
└──────────────────────┴───────┴──────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and ILIKE
Shorthand for the conditions you write most often




IN replaces a chain of OR comparisons
BETWEEN includes both ends: 2018, 2019 and 2020



duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, year,
           ROUND(value, 1) AS life_exp
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'life_expectancy'
      AND country IN ('Brazil', 'Japan', 'Germany')
      AND year BETWEEN 2018 AND 2020
    ORDER BY country, year
    LIMIT 5
""")

┌─────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ country │ year  │ life_exp │
│ varchar │ int16 │  double  │
├─────────┼───────┼──────────┤
│ Brazil  │  2018 │     75.6 │
│ Brazil  │  2019 │     75.8 │
│ Brazil  │  2020 │     74.5 │
│ Germany │  2018 │     80.9 │
│ Germany │  2019 │     81.3 │
└─────────┴───────┴──────────┘





LIKE matches a text pattern. % stands for any run of characters, _ for exactly one
ILIKE is the same test ignoring case (DuckDB only)



duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT DISTINCT country
    FROM wdi
    WHERE country LIKE 'United%'
""")

┌──────────────────────┐
│       country        │
│       varchar        │
├──────────────────────┤
│ United States        │
│ United Arab Emirates │
│ United Kingdom       │
└──────────────────────┘




Write 'united%' in lower case with plain LIKE and DuckDB returns zero rows. SQLite would return all three. The sqlite3 section has the full list of these differences

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: The order a query really runs in
text:
The order a query really runs in
How the engine evaluates a query







You write SELECT first, but the engine runs it fifth
FROM finds the rows, WHERE filters them, GROUP BY forms the groups, HAVING filters groups, then SELECT computes the output



An aggregate cannot go in WHERE: the groups do not exist yet
Standard SQL (and PostgreSQL) rejects a SELECT alias inside WHERE. DuckDB and SQLite accept it

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
GROUP BY
One row of output per group




An aggregate function reads many rows and returns one number

Without GROUP BY, the whole filtered table is one group

GROUP BY splits the rows into groups and applies the aggregate to each one
Every column in SELECT must be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate
Eight indicators, eight rows
primary_enrolment_net has 217 rows in 2020 and no values, so COUNT(value) is 0 and AVG is NULL
Mean population is 36 million, mean fertility 2.49: averaging across indicators would be meaningless
Grouping by two columns gives one row per pair: Appendix 05




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT indicator,
           COUNT(value) AS n,
           ROUND(AVG(value), 2) AS mean_value
    FROM wdi
    WHERE year = 2020
    GROUP BY indicator
    ORDER BY indicator
""")

┌───────────────────────┬───────┬─────────────┐
│       indicator       │   n   │ mean_value  │
│        varchar        │ int64 │   double    │
├───────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────┤
│ co2_per_capita        │   203 │        4.45 │
│ fertility_rate        │   217 │        2.49 │
│ gdp_per_capita        │   208 │    16149.94 │
│ internet_users_pct    │   184 │       64.11 │
│ life_expectancy       │   217 │        72.5 │
│ population            │   217 │ 36084236.48 │
│ primary_enrolment_net │     0 │        NULL │
│ urban_pop_pct         │   217 │       61.82 │
└───────────────────────┴───────┴─────────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
WHERE and HAVING
Filtering before and after grouping




WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after, so only HAVING can take an aggregate
WHERE year >= 2010 drops the old rows, HAVING AVG(value) > 60000 drops the poorer countries
“Which years count?” is a row question. “Which countries qualify?” is a group question
Small economies with financial centres dominate: Monaco, Liechtenstein and Bermuda all have under 100,000 people
ORDER BY can use an alias (mean_gdp here)




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country,
           ROUND(AVG(value), 0) AS mean_gdp
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita'
      AND year >= 2010
    GROUP BY country
    HAVING AVG(value) > 60000
    ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC
    LIMIT 5
""")

┌───────────────┬──────────┐
│    country    │ mean_gdp │
│    varchar    │  double  │
├───────────────┼──────────┤
│ Monaco        │ 173083.0 │
│ Liechtenstein │ 167187.0 │
│ Bermuda       │ 107724.0 │
│ Luxembourg    │ 106545.0 │
│ Switzerland   │  86948.0 │
└───────────────┴──────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
COUNT(*) and COUNT(value)
Counting rows and counting values




COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX cover almost everything you will write
COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(value) counts rows where value is present
AVG, SUM, MIN and MAX skip missing values silently
The difference between the two counts is the number of holes in the column
Internet use has 217 country rows in each year, but 9 values are missing in 1990, 21 in 2000 and 33 in 2020
Coverage gets worse over time: small territories join the panel and never report the series
Run this on any column before you trust its mean (SUMMARIZE does it for the whole file)




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT year,
           COUNT(*) AS n_rows,
           COUNT(value) AS with_value,
           COUNT(*) - COUNT(value) AS missing
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'internet_users_pct'
      AND year IN (1990, 2000, 2020)
    GROUP BY year
    ORDER BY year
""")

┌───────┬────────┬────────────┬─────────┐
│ year  │ n_rows │ with_value │ missing │
│ int16 │ int64  │   int64    │  int64  │
├───────┼────────┼────────────┼─────────┤
│  1990 │    217 │        208 │       9 │
│  2000 │    217 │        196 │      21 │
│  2020 │    217 │        184 │      33 │
└───────┴────────┴────────────┴─────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Try it yourself! 🧠
Five minutes



Which countries have had the highest life expectancy since 2010?

Open a Python file or a notebook
Import duckdb
Create the wdi view over ../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet
Keep only the rows for life_expectancy
Keep only the years from 2010 onwards
Compute the mean of value for each country
Keep the countries whose mean is above 82
Sort from highest to lowest
Return the top five, rounded to one decimal


What to look for:

The filter on year and the filter on the average go in different clauses. One of them is WHERE
ORDER BY can name the alias you created in SELECT
Five rows, all above 83 years. Four are small states or city economies
Japan is the only large country there, in fourth place
An error about an aggregate in WHERE? Re-read the evaluation-order ladder


Solution and the full output: Appendix 01

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Missing values
Working with NULL




A NULL means “unknown”, so it is neither zero nor an empty string
Test it with IS NULL, never with =
COALESCE(a, b) returns a, or b when a is NULL
We ask for five countries and get four rows: Somalia has no CO2 row at all for 2022
COALESCE cannot fix a missing row, only a missing value. A LEFT JOIN can (see the joins section)




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country,
           ROUND(COALESCE(value, 0), 1) AS co2_filled
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'co2_per_capita'
      AND year = 2022
      AND country IN ('Brazil', 'Japan', 'Somalia',
                      'Germany', 'Eritrea')
    ORDER BY country
""")

┌─────────┬────────────┐
│ country │ co2_filled │
│ varchar │   double   │
├─────────┼────────────┤
│ Brazil  │        2.3 │
│ Eritrea │        0.2 │
│ Germany │        7.9 │
│ Japan   │        8.4 │
└─────────┴────────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
CASE
Writing an if-else ladder inside a SELECT





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc,
        CASE
            WHEN value IS NULL  THEN 'No data'
            WHEN value >= 13846 THEN 'High income'
            WHEN value >= 4466  THEN 'Upper middle'
            WHEN value >= 1136  THEN 'Lower middle'
            ELSE 'Low income'
        END AS income_band
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020
      AND country IN ('Norway', 'China', 'India',
                      'Burundi', 'Brazil')
    ORDER BY value DESC NULLS LAST
""")

┌─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
│ country │ gdp_pc  │ income_band  │
│ varchar │ double  │   varchar    │
├─────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤
│ Norway  │ 78387.0 │ High income  │
│ China   │ 10573.0 │ Upper middle │
│ Brazil  │  8435.0 │ Upper middle │
│ India   │  1807.0 │ Lower middle │
│ Burundi │   263.0 │ Low income   │
└─────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘





CASE tests conditions in order and stops at the first true one, like if/elif
The thresholds are the World Bank’s income bands: 13,846, 4,466 and 1,136 dollars per person
The IS NULL test comes first on purpose: at the bottom, a missing value would fall through to ELSE and become “Low income”
ELSE catches everything else. Without it, unmatched rows get NULL
NULLS LAST sends unknown values to the bottom of the sort
The result is a new column you can group by, join on, or export

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Window functions
Adding a group-level number to every row





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc,
           ROUND(AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY year), 0)
               AS world_mean,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY value DESC) AS world_rank
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita'
      AND year = 2020 AND value IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY world_rank
    LIMIT 5
""")

┌─────────────┬──────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
│   country   │  gdp_pc  │ world_mean │ world_rank │
│   varchar   │  double  │   double   │   int64    │
├─────────────┼──────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
│ Monaco      │ 161263.0 │    16150.0 │          1 │
│ Luxembourg  │ 105274.0 │    16150.0 │          2 │
│ Bermuda     │  98846.0 │    16150.0 │          3 │
│ Isle of Man │  86595.0 │    16150.0 │          4 │
│ Switzerland │  86294.0 │    16150.0 │          5 │
└─────────────┴──────────┴────────────┴────────────┘





GROUP BY collapses each group to one row. A window function keeps every row and adds a value computed across the group
OVER turns a function into a window function. PARTITION BY year defines the group
world_mean is 16,150 on every row, the same as a plain AVG over 2020
RANK() needs an ORDER BY inside the OVER
All 208 countries survive this query; we print five

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Two small tables
Keys, and the two tables we will join






duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gdp2020 AS
    SELECT country, iso3, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_per_capita
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020
      AND iso3 IN ('USA','BRA','CHN','IND','DEU','JPN')
""")

duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE regions
        (iso3 VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, region VARCHAR)
""")

duckdb.sql("""
    INSERT INTO regions VALUES
        ('USA', 'North America'), ('BRA', 'Latin America'),
        ('CHN', 'East Asia'),     ('IND', 'South Asia'),
        ('DEU', 'Europe'),        ('KOR', 'East Asia')
""")

duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM regions ORDER BY iso3")

┌─────────┬───────────────┐
│  iso3   │    region     │
│ varchar │    varchar    │
├─────────┼───────────────┤
│ BRA     │ Latin America │
│ CHN     │ East Asia     │
│ DEU     │ Europe        │
│ IND     │ South Asia    │
│ KOR     │ East Asia     │
│ USA     │ North America │
└─────────┴───────────────┘






A table is a grid with named columns, one type per column
CREATE TABLE creates it, INSERT INTO ... VALUES adds rows
A primary key identifies a row uniquely (no duplicates, no NULLs): iso3 in regions
A foreign key points at another table’s primary key: iso3 in gdp2020. A join follows it with ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
Six rows on each side, with two mismatches: JPN has a GDP figure and no region, KOR a region and no GDP figure
East Asia holds two codes (this matters for the second exercise)

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
INNER JOIN
Only the rows that match on both sides





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT g.country, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita
    FROM gdp2020 AS g
    INNER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
    ORDER BY g.country
""")

┌───────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
│    country    │    region     │ gdp_per_capita │
│    varchar    │    varchar    │     double     │
├───────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Brazil        │ Latin America │         8435.0 │
│ China         │ East Asia     │        10573.0 │
│ Germany       │ Europe        │        42373.0 │
│ India         │ South Asia    │         1807.0 │
│ United States │ North America │        59534.0 │
└───────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘





ON says which columns must agree: the iso3 code on each side
AS g and AS r are table aliases, so g.iso3 and r.iso3 stay apart
Six rows on the left, six on the right, five rows out
Japan has no matching region, Korea no matching GDP row, so both drop out
An inner join is a silent filter: if your row count falls after a join, this is usually why

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
LEFT JOIN
Keeping every row of the left table





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT g.country, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita
    FROM gdp2020 AS g
    LEFT JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
    ORDER BY g.country
""")

┌───────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
│    country    │    region     │ gdp_per_capita │
│    varchar    │    varchar    │     double     │
├───────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Brazil        │ Latin America │         8435.0 │
│ China         │ East Asia     │        10573.0 │
│ Germany       │ Europe        │        42373.0 │
│ India         │ South Asia    │         1807.0 │
│ Japan         │ NULL          │        35363.0 │
│ United States │ North America │        59534.0 │
└───────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘





The join you will use most often
Six rows now: Japan is back, with NULL in region
The NULL means the join found no partner
LEFT is the table named in FROM. Swap the two tables and you get a different answer
Korea is still missing, because it only exists in the right table

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
FULL OUTER JOIN
Every row from both tables survives





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT g.country, r.iso3 AS region_iso3,
           r.region, g.gdp_per_capita
    FROM gdp2020 AS g
    FULL OUTER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
    ORDER BY r.region NULLS LAST
""")

┌───────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
│    country    │ region_iso3 │    region     │ gdp_per_capita │
│    varchar    │   varchar   │    varchar    │     double     │
├───────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
│ China         │ CHN         │ East Asia     │        10573.0 │
│ NULL          │ KOR         │ East Asia     │           NULL │
│ Germany       │ DEU         │ Europe        │        42373.0 │
│ Brazil        │ BRA         │ Latin America │         8435.0 │
│ United States │ USA         │ North America │        59534.0 │
│ India         │ IND         │ South Asia    │         1807.0 │
│ Japan         │ NULL        │ NULL          │        35363.0 │
└───────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘







The picture uses cut-down tables, so its counts are 3, 4 and 5. Ours give 5, 6 and 7




Every row from both tables appears, with NULLs where the other side has no partner
Seven rows: five matched, plus Korea (no GDP) and Japan (no region)
Just to recap: 5 rows from INNER, 6 from LEFT, 7 from FULL OUTER
To choose a join, ask which table must survive whole and what should happen to rows with no partner

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Try it yourself! 🧠
Ten minutes

Querying a DataFrame by name
Your Python variable becomes a SQL table

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Why sqlite3
Assignment 09 uses SQLite, and it ships with Python




SQLite is a database in a single file, with no server

The most deployed database in the world: every phone and every browser carries a copy

Python bundles it, so import sqlite3 works on a machine with nothing installed
The cost is boilerplate DuckDB never asked for: a connection, a cursor, commit() and fetchall()

A connection links your script to the database file. A cursor sends commands and collects results

The SQL itself barely changes. The next slides re-run queries you have already seen





Source: https://sqlite.org

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Loading the panel into SQLite
Writing a DataFrame into a table





import sqlite3

# ":memory:" builds the database in RAM.
# Use a filename such as "wdi.db" to keep it
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

df.to_sql("wdi", conn, index=False,
          if_exists="replace")

pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM wdi", conn)








n




0
59024










to_sql writes a DataFrame into a table and picks the column types for you
index=False stops the pandas index becoming a column called index
if_exists="replace" drops any old table of that name, so the cell is safe to re-run
pd.read_sql sends a query and returns a DataFrame, with no cursor and no fetchall
The load took 0.03 seconds for 59,024 rows on my laptop
Categories need no cast here, unlike the DuckDB enum

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Connection, cursor, commit, fetch
The sqlite3 boilerplate





cur = conn.cursor()

cur.execute("""CREATE TABLE regions
               (iso3 TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT)""")

cur.executemany("INSERT INTO regions VALUES (?, ?)",
    [("USA", "North America"), ("BRA", "Latin America"),
     ("CHN", "East Asia"),     ("IND", "South Asia"),
     ("DEU", "Europe"),        ("KOR", "East Asia")])
conn.commit()

cur.execute("""SELECT iso3, region FROM regions
               WHERE region = ? ORDER BY iso3""",
            ("East Asia",))
print(cur.fetchall())

cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM regions")
print(cur.fetchone())

[('CHN', 'East Asia'), ('KOR', 'East Asia')]
(6,)





executemany runs one SQL template over a list of tuples
The ? marks a slot the driver fills in safely (Python’s None becomes SQL’s NULL)

Never build a query with an f-string: that is how SQL injection happens

commit() makes the writes permanent. Skip it and the inserts vanish when the script ends
fetchall() returns a list of tuples, fetchone() a single tuple, e.g. (6,)
Parameters must be a tuple, hence the trailing comma in ("East Asia",)

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
DuckDB on 200 million rows
The lecture 21 benchmark, revisited

















Task: mean value by indicator and decade since 1990, on wdi_big.parquet, a synthetic panel of 200,681,600 rows
DuckDB: 0.53 s. Dask: 5.39 s. pandas: 9.65 s
pandas loads every column into RAM. DuckDB reads only the row groups and columns the query names
Why: columnar layout, vectorised execution, all cores by default, and predicate pushdown into the Parquet file
MacBook Pro, Apple M5, 10 cores, 24 GB RAM, macOS 26.6
One task on one machine: your seconds will differ, the ranking usually holds
Polars is in the same range as DuckDB (see Tutorial 07 on the course website)
The query and the scripts behind it: Appendix 08

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What we learned today
The vocabulary, in the order we met it




SQL is declarative: you describe the answer and the engine plans the work
DuckDB needs one import and reads a Parquet file or a pandas DataFrame by name
A view names a query. DESCRIBE and SUMMARIZE show what is in it
WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups. No aggregate in WHERE
COUNT(*) minus COUNT(value) is the number of missing values



A NULL means unknown. COALESCE fills one in, and a missing row needs a join instead
CASE builds a category column. A window function keeps every row and adds a group-level number
Joins: 5 rows from INNER, 6 from LEFT, 7 from FULL OUTER on the same two tables
sqlite3 needs a connection, a cursor, commit() and fetchall(), but the SQL is the same
On 200 million rows, DuckDB runs the same query in 0.53 seconds

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 01: Solution to Exercise 01





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country,
           ROUND(AVG(value), 1) AS mean_life_exp
    FROM wdi
    WHERE indicator = 'life_expectancy'
      AND year >= 2010
    GROUP BY country
    HAVING AVG(value) > 82
    ORDER BY mean_life_exp DESC
    LIMIT 5
""")

┌──────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│       country        │ mean_life_exp │
│       varchar        │    double     │
├──────────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ Monaco               │          85.5 │
│ San Marino           │          84.4 │
│ Hong Kong SAR, China │          84.3 │
│ Andorra              │          83.8 │
│ Japan                │          83.8 │
└──────────────────────┴───────────────┘





WHERE drops the rows before 2010 and every other indicator
GROUP BY country forms one group per country
HAVING AVG(value) > 82 tests the group, so it cannot be written in WHERE
ORDER BY names mean_life_exp, the alias created in SELECT
Monaco, San Marino and Andorra are microstates with small, wealthy, ageing populations
Japan is the only country in the list with more than a million people

Back to the exercise

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 02: Solution to Exercise 02





duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT r.region,
           COUNT(g.country) AS countries_with_gdp,
           ROUND(AVG(g.gdp_per_capita), 0) AS mean_gdp
    FROM regions AS r
    LEFT JOIN gdp2020 AS g ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
    GROUP BY r.region
    ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC NULLS LAST
""")

┌───────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────┐
│    region     │ countries_with_gdp │ mean_gdp │
│    varchar    │       int64        │  double  │
├───────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────┤
│ North America │                  1 │  59534.0 │
│ Europe        │                  1 │  42373.0 │
│ East Asia     │                  1 │  10573.0 │
│ Latin America │                  1 │   8435.0 │
│ South Asia    │                  1 │   1807.0 │
└───────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────┘




regions goes on the left because every region must survive
COUNT(g.country) skips the NULLs a left join produces. COUNT(*) would count Korea’s empty row and report 2 for East Asia


The optional part:


duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT COALESCE(g.iso3, r.iso3) AS iso3,
           g.country, r.region
    FROM gdp2020 AS g
    FULL OUTER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3
    WHERE g.iso3 IS NULL OR r.iso3 IS NULL
    ORDER BY iso3
""")

┌─────────┬─────────┬───────────┐
│  iso3   │ country │  region   │
│ varchar │ varchar │  varchar  │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────────┤
│ JPN     │ Japan   │ NULL      │
│ KOR     │ NULL    │ East Asia │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────────┘




COALESCE picks up whichever code exists, because one of the two is always NULL here

Back to the exercise

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 03: When something goes wrong



Parser Error: syntax error at or near ".."
The file path is not quoted. Put single quotes around it: FROM '../data/f.parquet'.
IO Error: No files found that match the pattern
The path is quoted but wrong. Paths are relative to the folder you launched Python in, so check with os.getcwd().
Binder Error: Referenced column "gdp" not found
The column name is misspelled or does not exist. Run DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM wdi and read the list.
Parser Error: syntax error at or near "SELCT"
A keyword is misspelled. DuckDB quotes the offending word back at you, so read the message to the end

Binder Error on a value you know exists
You wrote WHERE indicator = "gdp_per_capita" with double quotes. Double quotes mean a column name in SQL, single quotes mean text.
sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table: wdi
The table was never created in this connection. :memory: databases vanish when the script ends, so re-run the to_sql cell.
sqlite3.OperationalError: no such column: gdp
Same as the DuckDB binder error. List the columns with PRAGMA table_info(wdi).
Your inserts disappeared
You forgot conn.commit(). SQLite holds writes in a transaction until you commit them

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 04: The complete sqlite3 listing


Everything from the sqlite3 section in one script, ready to adapt for assignment 09:

import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

# 1. Connect. Use a filename to keep the database on disk
conn = sqlite3.connect("wdi.db")
cur = conn.cursor()

# 2. Load a DataFrame into a table
df = pd.read_parquet("../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet")
df.to_sql("wdi", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

# 3. Create a table by hand and fill it
cur.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS regions")
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE regions (iso3 TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT)")
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO regions VALUES (?, ?)",
    [("USA", "North America"), ("BRA", "Latin America"),
     ("CHN", "East Asia"),     ("IND", "South Asia"),
     ("DEU", "Europe"),        ("KOR", "East Asia")])
conn.commit()

# 4. Query with a cursor: fetchall returns a list of tuples
cur.execute("SELECT iso3, region FROM regions WHERE region = ?", ("East Asia",))
print(cur.fetchall())

# 5. Query into pandas instead
out = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT r.region, COUNT(w.value) AS n, ROUND(AVG(w.value), 0) AS mean_gdp
    FROM regions AS r
    LEFT JOIN wdi AS w
      ON w.iso3 = r.iso3
     AND w.indicator = 'gdp_per_capita'
     AND w.year = 2020
    GROUP BY r.region
    ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC
""", conn)
print(out)

# 6. Close the connection when you are done
conn.close()

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 05: Grouping by two columns
Every combination that exists in the data




Name two columns and you get one row for each pair that appears in the filtered rows
Two countries and two indicators give four rows here
Combinations with no rows never appear. SQL does not invent empty groups
Japan’s mean life expectancy since 2010 is nine years above Brazil’s. Its CO2 per person is almost four times higher
Aggregating a mean of yearly means like this weights every year equally. Say so when you report it




duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, indicator,
           ROUND(AVG(value), 1) AS mean_value
    FROM wdi
    WHERE year >= 2010
      AND country IN ('Brazil', 'Japan')
      AND indicator IN ('life_expectancy',
                        'co2_per_capita')
    GROUP BY country, indicator
    ORDER BY country, indicator
""")

┌─────────┬─────────────────┬────────────┐
│ country │    indicator    │ mean_value │
│ varchar │     varchar     │   double   │
├─────────┼─────────────────┼────────────┤
│ Brazil  │ co2_per_capita  │        2.4 │
│ Brazil  │ life_expectancy │       74.8 │
│ Japan   │ co2_per_capita  │        9.3 │
│ Japan   │ life_expectancy │       83.8 │
└─────────┴─────────────────┴────────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 06: Anti-joins and UNION
Finding rows with no partner




An anti-join asks which rows on the left have no partner on the right
NOT EXISTS runs a small query for each row and keeps the row when it returns nothing



duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT g.country, g.iso3
    FROM gdp2020 AS g
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM regions AS r
        WHERE r.iso3 = g.iso3
    )
""")

┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ country │  iso3   │
│ varchar │ varchar │
├─────────┼─────────┤
│ Japan   │ JPN     │
└─────────┴─────────┘





A join adds columns. UNION stacks rows from two results that have the same columns
UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps them and is faster



duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT country, 'rich' AS tag FROM gdp2020
    WHERE gdp_per_capita > 30000
    UNION
    SELECT country, 'poor' AS tag FROM gdp2020
    WHERE gdp_per_capita < 10000
    ORDER BY country
""")

┌───────────────┬─────────┐
│    country    │   tag   │
│    varchar    │ varchar │
├───────────────┼─────────┤
│ Brazil        │ poor    │
│ Germany       │ rich    │
│ India         │ poor    │
│ Japan         │ rich    │
│ United States │ rich    │
└───────────────┴─────────┘

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Appendix 07: When SQL beats a DataFrame
text:
Appendix 07: When SQL beats a DataFrame
A checklist for each tool



Reach for SQL when:

You are joining two or more tables
You are filtering and aggregating a file that is larger than your RAM
The question is a GROUP BY with a couple of conditions
Someone else has to read the query. A colleague who has never seen pandas can still read your SELECT
The data already lives in a database


Stay in pandas when:

You need row-by-row logic that has no set-based version
You are plotting, or feeding a model
You want many small inspectable steps, each one a variable you can look at
The reshaping is the hard part, as in the pivot in the SQL in Python section


Want more practice? The course website has a full self-study DuckDB SQL tutorial covering everything on these slides in more depth

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 08: The benchmark query
The query and where the timings come from




The DuckDB version is the query you already know, with a file path in FROM and a GROUP BY at the end
The data is wdi_big.parquet, a synthetic panel of 200,681,600 rows built by cloning the small panel many times
The file is not committed, and the script that rebuilds it is in data/make_big_parquet.py
The timings were measured once and saved to data/benchmark_results.csv. The deck reads that file rather than re-running anything
pandas loads the whole thing and calls groupby, Dask uses a parallel DataFrame, and DuckDB runs SQL straight over the file




import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT indicator,
           (year // 10) * 10 AS decade,
           AVG(value) AS mean_value
    FROM 'data/wdi_big.parquet'
    WHERE year >= 1990
    GROUP BY indicator, decade
""").df()

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Congratulations! 🎉
You have a project 🥳




Your code works, it is fast thanks to Polars and DuckDB, the report renders, the repository is documented
One question remains: will it run anywhere else?
What happens when you move it to a new machine, hand it to a colleague, or open it again in six months?
Everything so far assumed one thing you never wrote down: the software installed on your laptop
Dependency management makes that assumption explicit

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Why do we need dependency management?
text:
Why do we need dependency management?



The problem

Libraries change constantly!
Even very simple code breaks when software updates
From Python 2.x to 3.x:

-c means “run this command”



python2 -c 'print "Hello, DATASCI350!"'
Hello, DATASCI350!

python3 -c 'print "Hello, DATASCI350!"'

  File "<string>", line 1
    print "Hello, DATASCI350!"
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to
'print'. Did you mean print(...)?


Some definitions


Dependency management: making sure your code will run in the future
Dependencies: external libraries, packages, and software your code needs
Packages: have a name, a version, and possibly their own dependencies
Package registry: a directory that stores packages and metadata, e.g., CRAN, PyPI, Conda
Dependency management tools: pip, conda, and others install and track those packages
Every tool in this lecture exists to write that list down and replay it somewhere else

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The reproducibility crisis




Reproducibility crisis: many researchers cannot replicate published results
It affects computer science, statistics, psychology, and medicine alike
Some causes are statistical: p-hacking, publication bias, low power
A 2016 Nature survey asked 1,576 researchers:

More than 70% had failed to reproduce another scientist’s experiment
More than half had failed to reproduce one of their own

Missing documentation and unrecorded dependencies are as common, and both have a technical fix
The rest of today is that fix

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The reproducibility trade-off
How far do you go?





How far should you go to make a result reproducible? It depends on who has to rerun it
At minimum, declare your dependencies so others know what you used
Manage them with a package or environment manager (conda, pip, uv)
Pin them with renv (R) or uv (Python), which record exact versions
Host them online with Code Ocean ($$$) or Binder (free and limited)
Go further with containers (Docker, Apptainer) for full portability
Your project sits near the right-hand end, and the rest of today is how to get there

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
How to declare dependencies?
One file in the repository root


Say your analysis uses Python, NumPy, pandas, and matplotlib. Ask yourself:

What packages do I need?
Will this work on my collaborator’s operating system?
Can someone else reproduce my results?

Use a package manager to declare your dependencies in a single file
Store it in the repository root so collaborators can install everything in one step
Which file depends on your package manager:

pip (Python only): requirements.txt
conda (Python and R): environment.yml
uv (Python only): pyproject.toml and uv.lock

Know requirements.txt best: every Dockerfile reads it, including your project starter’s
Let’s see all three

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: venv and pip: an isolated Python
text:
venv and pip: an isolated Python
The workflow your Dockerfile will use




venv ships with Python. It creates a folder with its own python and site-packages
Nothing you install inside it touches the system Python
Two projects can keep two versions of the same package
Create it, switch into it, and install:


python3 -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate    # macOS and Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate       # Windows

pip install requests polars


Add .venv/ to your .gitignore. The package list goes into git; the folder itself stays on your machine



which python tells you which interpreter you are actually using:


which python
/private/tmp/[...]/l23/venv-demo/.venv/bin/python

python --version
Python 3.14.6

pip --version
pip 26.1.2 [...] (python 3.14)


The path ends in .venv/bin/python, so the environment is active
The install itself:


Successfully installed certifi-2026.7.22
charset_normalizer-3.5.1 idna-3.19 polars-1.44.0
polars-runtime-32-1.44.0 requests-2.34.2
urllib3-2.7.0


Docker images do this too
The project starter’s Dockerfile runs python3 -m venv /opt/venv and sets ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH", so every later instruction uses that interpreter without activation

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
requirements.txt: the file you commit
pip freeze writes it and pip install -r reads it




Inside the clean environment, pip freeze prints every installed package with its exact version:

pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt

certifi==2026.7.22
charset-normalizer==3.5.1
idna==3.19
polars==1.44.0
polars-runtime-32==1.44.0
requests==2.34.2
urllib3==2.7.0

Two packages became seven lines because pip lists the dependencies of your dependencies
The == pins say “these exact versions”



Your collaborator makes their own environment and installs from the file:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Run pip freeze inside a conda environment and some lines come out as name @ file:///... local paths, which install nowhere else
Freeze inside a plain venv and the problem never appears
Our project starter repo pins every package by hand, with a comment for each:

# Talking to web APIs
requests==2.34.2

# Data processing (use either, or both)
polars==1.44.0
duckdb==1.5.5

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Conda in one slide
You met conda in DATASCI 151




Conda manages environments and packages together, and installs non-Python software: compilers, R, CUDA
Create it and switch into it:


conda create --name l23-demo \
  python=3.14 numpy pandas -y
conda activate l23-demo


Export it with --from-history, which records only the packages you asked for:


conda env export --name l23-demo \
  --from-history > environment.yml


Others recreate it with conda env create --file environment.yml, then conda activate l23-demo



The file it produced:


name: l23-demo
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - defaults
dependencies:
  - pandas
  - numpy
  - python=3.14
prefix: /Users/dafreir/miniconda3/envs/l23-demo


Drop --from-history and it lists every transitive package instead:


  - _openmp_mutex=4.5=7_kmp_llvm
  - bzip2=1.0.8=h4e30115_10
  - libblas=3.11.0=9_h51639a9_openblas
  - libcxx=23.1.0=h55c6f16_0
  [...]


Those files describe one machine exactly but rarely install on another. The next slide takes one apart

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What are build strings?
Reading a conda package specification




A conda build is a specific compiled binary of a package
The same version can be compiled differently per platform, Python version, or feature set
A full conda package specification:

numpy=1.21.5=py39h12345_0
└──┬─┘└─┬──┘ └────┬───┘└┬┘
   │    │         │     │
   │    │         │     └─ Build number (0)
   │    │         └─────── Build string (py39h12345)
   │    └───────────────── Version (1.21.5)
   └────────────────────── Package name (numpy)

The --no-builds flag strips it, making the file portable across platforms



The build string (py39h12345) encodes metadata:

Python version (py39, py310)
Architecture (linux_64, osx_arm64)
Compiler (gcc9, clang)
Features (nomkl, cuda)

Why do builds exist?

Software is compiled differently per operating system
Packages target specific Python versions
Builds enable or disable optional features
Different compilers produce different binaries

The line libblas=3.11.0=9_h51639a9_openblas on the previous slide will not resolve on a Linux collaborator’s machine

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: uv: a fast Python package manager
text:
uv: a fast Python package manager
Maybe new to you




uv is a Python package and project manager built by Astral, the people behind the Ruff linter
Written in Rust, it replaces pip, pip-tools, pipenv, poetry, virtualenv, and pyenv with one command
It installs Python itself, so you need no separate installer
Install it:

# macOS and Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# or with Homebrew
brew install uv

uv --version
uv 0.11.7 (9d177269e 2026-04-15
aarch64-apple-darwin)





https://docs.astral.sh/uv/


uv init l23-uv-demo --python 3.14
cd l23-uv-demo
uv add polars requests

Using CPython 3.14.6 interpreter at:
  /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/bin/python3.14
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 8 packages in 1.62s
Prepared 3 packages in 1m 06s
Installed 7 packages in 12ms
 + polars==1.44.0
 [...]
 + requests==2.34.2


Eight packages resolved in 1.62 seconds, environment created along the way

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
uv: project files and sharing
Just two files, and both belong in git




pyproject.toml holds your direct dependencies and is meant for humans. Mine after uv add:

[project]
name = "l23-uv-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "polars>=1.44.0",
    "requests>=2.34.2",
]

TOML (Tom’s Obvious Minimal Language): a config format of key-value pairs and [sections]. Created by Tom Preston-Werner, a GitHub co-founder. More here

Very similar to YAML, which we saw when writing Quarto documents

uv init also writes a .gitignore, a README.md, and a main.py



uv.lock is generated for you, recording the exact version and hash of every package
Mine is 182 lines for eight packages. You never edit it by hand
Push both pyproject.toml and uv.lock. Your collaborator clones and runs uv sync to get the same environment:

uv sync
Resolved 8 packages in 2ms
Checked 7 packages in 1ms

uv run python -c \
  "import polars; print(polars.__version__)"
1.44.0

uv run executes inside the project environment, so there is nothing to activate
uv manages Python versions too: uv python install 3.14 and uv python pin 3.14
More about uv here

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: uv: handing a project to Docker
text:
uv: handing a project to Docker
Every Dockerfile still wants requirements.txt




Docker images read requirements.txt, and uv export writes one from your lock file:

uv export --format requirements-txt --no-hashes

Resolved 8 packages in 2ms
# This file was autogenerated by uv via the
# following command:
#    uv export --format requirements-txt
#      --no-hashes
certifi==2026.7.22
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.5.1
    # via requests
polars==1.44.0
    # via l23-uv-demo
requests==2.34.2
    # via l23-uv-demo
[...]

Drop --no-hashes and each line also carries the wheel’s SHA-256, which pip then verifies



Redirect it into the file your Dockerfile copies:

uv export --format requirements-txt \
  --no-hashes > requirements.txt

The # via comments name which package pulled each dependency in. pip freeze never does
Want the venv and pip workflow at uv’s speed? Drop-in replacements:

uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

Same commands, same files as the venv slides, with uv doing the install

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The matrix from hell





Each cell is one combination someone has to test by hand

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Cargo transport before 1960





Sacks, barrels, and crates, each loaded differently at every port

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Also a matrix from hell





Shipping had the same combinatorial problem

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The solution: intermodal containers





A standard box fits every ship, train, and lorry, and nobody opens it in transit

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Docker is a container for your code
text:
Docker is a container for your code





Your code, its libraries, and its Python version inside a container

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Docker eliminates the matrix from hell
text:
Docker eliminates the matrix from hell





The host only needs Docker, and the image carries everything else

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What are software containers?
Lighter than a virtual machine




Containers package software so it can run on any system
A virtual machine boots a whole operating system. A container carries only the libraries the application needs, so it starts in a second
A virtual environment isolates Python packages. A container also carries the operating system libraries, the interpreter, and the system tools your code touches
It then runs on any system with Docker installed, whatever the operating system or hardware



Created with tools like Docker or Apptainer
Usually a stripped-down Linux (Ubuntu or Alpine Linux) with only the required libraries
Why Linux? It is open source and the most widely used server operating system
Stored in container registries like Docker Hub, so you can share them
More about Docker here


Lecture 10 listed four ingredients of a reproducible result: code, data, environment, documentation. A container ships the environment with the code already inside it

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
What is Docker?
Images, containers, and registries




Docker is the leading containerisation platform
Three concepts that you should know:

Image: a read-only template holding the operating system, the libraries, your code, and the configuration. You build images from a Dockerfile
Container: a running instance of an image. Many containers from one image
Registry: a collection of repositories you pull images from, such as Docker Hub

An image is a class and a container is an object (more here)
The syntax borrows from Git and Linux, so it should feel familiar
The docker command is a client. It sends every instruction to a background daemon, which does the building and the running






Client, daemon, and registry, from the Docker documentation

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Docker Desktop and the alternatives




Docker Desktop runs the Docker engine on macOS and Windows. It is how most of you will install Docker

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The Dockerfile
Five instructions and five layers



# Start from an official Python image
FROM python:3.14-slim

# Everything below happens inside /app
WORKDIR /app

# Copy requirements first, so Docker can
# cache the install
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy the script
COPY hello.py .

# What runs when the container starts
CMD ["python", "hello.py"]

--no-cache-dir -r means “install from the file and don’t keep a cache of the wheels”
Let’s build it! -t tags the image datasci350-example, and . is the folder holding the Dockerfile:

docker build -t datasci350-example .


docker build runs the instructions in sequence, layer by layer, and each one adds a layer





Instruction
What it does
Runs when

Picks the base image
Build


WORKDIR
Sets the folder for every later step
Build


COPY
Brings a file from your folder into the image
Build


RUN
Executes a command inside the image
Build


CMD
Names the command the container starts with
Start

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Layer caching
Why the second build takes no time at all




Run the same build again, changing nothing:

docker build -t datasci350-example .

#5 [1/5] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.14-slim
#5 DONE 0.0s

#6 [3/5] COPY requirements.txt .
#6 CACHED

#7 [4/5] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r
    requirements.txt
#7 CACHED

#8 [2/5] WORKDIR /app
#8 CACHED

#9 [5/5] COPY hello.py .
#9 CACHED

#10 exporting to image
#10 DONE 0.1s


Every layer says CACHED and the build finishes in 0.754 seconds
Docker reuses a layer when its instruction and its inputs are unchanged
Once one layer misses, every layer below it rebuilds
That is why COPY requirements.txt sits above COPY hello.py: editing your script invalidates only the last layer, and the slow pip install stays cached
Put COPY . . at the top and any edit re-installs every package
Your project starter’s Dockerfile uses the same ordering, for the same reason
Docker also reorders independent steps, which is why the cached run reports #6 as step [3/5]

text:
Appendix 02: When something goes wrong
Six errors you are likely to meet



Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
Docker Desktop is not running. Start the application, wait for the whale icon to settle, and try again. On my laptop OrbStack was stopped, and docker info answered failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///Users/dafreir/.orbstack/run/docker.sock.
permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock
On Linux, your user is not in the docker group. Run sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in.
pip: command not found
Your virtual environment is not active. Run source .venv/bin/activate and check with which python, which should print a path ending in .venv/bin/python.

No matching distribution found for numpy==2.5.2
That version does not exist for your Python. Check the pin against PyPI, or loosen it to numpy>=2.0.
toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit
Docker Hub allows 100 anonymous pulls per hour from one address. Run docker login with your free account and pull again.
failed to read dockerfile: open Dockerfile: no such file or directory
You are in the wrong folder. The . at the end of docker build -t name . is where Docker looks, so cd into the folder holding the Dockerfile

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: The whole file at a glance
text:
The whole file at a glance
Seven blocks, fourteen instructions, eight build steps




# 1. Base image
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# 2. Build-time settings
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]

# 3. System packages
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y [...]

# 4. Quarto
ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.37
RUN ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture) && [...]

# 5. Python environment
RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt /project/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /project/requirements.txt

# 6. Project files
WORKDIR /project
COPY . /project

# 7. Default command
ENV QUARTO_PYTHON=/opt/venv/bin/python
CMD ["bash", "-c", "quarto render report.qmd && [...]"]



Fourteen instructions in seven commented blocks
Only eight of them create a filesystem layer, which is why the build log counts [1/8] to [8/8]
ENV, ARG, SHELL, and CMD set metadata, so BuildKit does not number them
The comments in the real file are longer than the instructions. Read them once, and change only what you need


Lecture 23’s file had five instructions and one job: install two packages, run a script. This one installs an operating system, a document engine, and a Python environment in fourteen


Full listing

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Blocks 1 and 2: FROM, ENV, SHELL
Ubuntu 24.04, no questions asked




# We pin the tag to "24.04" rather than "latest".
# "latest" changes over time, and a base image
# that changes breaks reproducibility.
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive stops apt-get
# from asking questions during the build.
# Nobody is at the keyboard to answer them.
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Use bash for the RUN steps below. Docker uses
# the simpler "sh" shell by default.
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]


latest on the Ubuntu repository resolved to 24.04 last year. Today it resolves to 26.04
FROM ubuntu:latest in September builds a different operating system in December
tzdata is the package that would otherwise stop and ask you for a time zone






hub.docker.com/_/ubuntu, accessed 26 August 2026


ENV persists into the running container, so docker run sees it too
SHELL changes the shell for every RUN below it, so $(...) and && behave as you expect


ubuntu:24.04 is 139MB on disk here, 30.8MB compressed, against 204MB and 45.9MB for Lecture 23’s python:3.14-slim. It ships no Python at all, and Quarto arrives as a .deb, so we need the full Debian userland

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Block 3: RUN apt-get install
System packages in one layer




RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates \
    wget \
    git \
    python3.12 \
    python3.12-venv \
    python3-pip && \
    apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*


One RUN is one layer. Splitting this into six RUN lines would give six layers and a bigger image
apt-get clean and rm -rf delete the download cache. They have to run in the same layer, because a later layer cannot shrink an earlier one
--no-install-recommends skips optional extras
This step took 70.8 seconds cold






Package
Why




ca-certificates
HTTPS downloads fail without it


wget
Fetches the Quarto .deb


git
Some Quarto extensions want it


python3.12
The interpreter, version 3.12.3 here


python3.12-venv
Ubuntu ships venv separately


python3-pip
Installs into the virtual environment





An older version of this lecture pinned every apt package by hand, and the build broke the week Ubuntu shipped a security update, because the pinned version no longer existed in the archive. The starter pins the base image tag and the Python packages instead, and lets apt give you the current patch of each system package

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Block 4: Quarto
ARG, dpkg --print-architecture, and a .deb




ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.37
RUN ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture) && \
    wget -q "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends "./quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    rm "quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*


Quarto is not in the Ubuntu package list, so we download the .deb from GitHub
The build printed this near the end of the step:


#8 206.0 Setting up quarto (1.9.37) ...
#8 DONE 206.5s


206.5 seconds, the slowest step in the whole build
The ./ in front of the filename tells apt to install a local file rather than search the archive
apt-get update runs a second time because block 3 deleted the package lists



ARG is a build-time variable. Override it without editing the file:

docker build --build-arg QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.38 \
  -t datasci350-project .

ARG disappears when the build ends. ENV stays in the running container
dpkg --print-architecture printed arm64 on my Mac, amd64 on most Windows and Linux laptops. The same Dockerfile fetches the other file


This laptop has Quarto 1.9.38. The image has 1.9.37, because that is what the ARG says. The version inside the image renders your report, and it is the one I will run

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
section: Block 5: the virtual environment and pip
text:
Block 5: the virtual environment and pip
The layer order that makes rebuilds fast




# Ubuntu protects its own Python installation,
# so we create a virtual environment at
# /opt/venv and install our packages there.
RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv

# PATH tells the shell where to look for
# programs. Putting /opt/venv/bin first means
# "python" and "pip" refer to the virtual
# environment, without activating it by hand.
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

# We copy requirements.txt on its own, before
# the rest of the project.
COPY requirements.txt /project/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /project/requirements.txt



This is Lecture 23’s venv slide, moved inside an image. The ENV PATH line replaces source .venv/bin/activate
Ubuntu refuses a system-wide pip install and tells you to make a virtual environment. The error is externally-managed-environment: Appendix 02
--no-cache-dir stops pip keeping a copy of every wheel inside the image
The install took 89.2 seconds and produced 54 packages
COPY requirements.txt sits alone above COPY . /project so that editing report.qmd leaves this slow step cached


That ordering is the most useful thing in the file, and it pays off on the rebuild slide: jump there

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Blocks 6 and 7: WORKDIR, COPY ., CMD
Rendering into /project, copying into output/




# WORKDIR sets the folder that later
# instructions run inside.
WORKDIR /project

# Copy everything else from your repository into
# the image, including report.qmd and the saved
# data snapshot in data/raw/.
# The .dockerignore file next to this one lists
# what stays out.
COPY . /project

# QUARTO_PYTHON points Quarto at the virtual
# environment's Python.
ENV QUARTO_PYTHON=/opt/venv/bin/python
CMD ["bash", "-c", "quarto render report.qmd && mkdir -p output && cp -a report.html output/ && echo 'Rendered report is in output/report.html'"]



COPY . /project copies the build context, which is the folder you named with the . in docker build. The next slide keeps things out of it
Without QUARTO_PYTHON, Quarto looks for a system Python and misses the packages you installed
The CMD is three commands joined with &&: render, make output/, copy the HTML in
Quarto clears its output folder before writing, and it cannot clear a folder Docker has mounted from outside. Rendering into /project and copying afterwards avoids that


Lecture 23’s CMD ["python", "hello.py"] was the same exec form: a JSON array of strings, with no shell involved. Here the array starts bash, and bash provides the shell we need for &&

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
.dockerignore
What never enters the image




# Version control
.git

# Python environments and caches
.venv/
venv/
__pycache__/

# Quarto working files and rendered output
.quarto/
*.quarto_ipynb
report.html
report_files/
output/

# Operating system clutter
.DS_Store

# NOTE: data/raw/ is deliberately absent. The
# snapshot must reach the image, because
# report.qmd reads it.



Docker sends the whole context to the build engine before the first instruction runs. Two builds of the same folder, one with the file and one without:


=== WITHOUT .dockerignore ===
#3 load .dockerignore:      2B done
#5 load build context:      1.42MB done

=== WITH .dockerignore ===
#3 load .dockerignore:      578B done
#5 load build context:      59.36kB done


1.42MB down to 59.36kB, and both folders held .git, the snapshot, and a rendered output/report.html
.gitignore keeps files out of your repository. .dockerignore keeps them out of your image. data/raw/ belongs in neither


Leave report.html out of the list and every render changes the context, which breaks the cache on COPY . /project even when your source did not move

IMAGE                      DISK USAGE  CONTENT SIZE
datasci350-project:latest      1.64GB         368MB

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Running the container
One flag decides whether you ever see the report




time docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/output:/project/output" \
  datasci350-project

Starting python3 kernel...Done

Executing 'report.quarto_ipynb'
  Cell 1/1: 'fig-demo'...Done
[...]
Output created: report.html

Rendered report is in output/report.html
docker run [...]  2.980 total

ls -la output

-rw-r--r--  1 dafreir  wheel  1313598  report.html


Three seconds, because the slow work happened at build time










Part
What it does




--rm
Deletes the container when it exits


-v host:container
Connects a folder on your machine to one inside the container


datasci350-project
The image to start





-v is short for volume. The left side of the colon is your laptop, the right side is the container
$(pwd) is your current folder. PowerShell wants ${PWD} and the old Windows terminal wants %cd%
The path on the left must be absolute, which is why nobody writes -v ./output:...
The report is the only thing that survives the container, and it survives because of that flag


docker run creates a container from the image and starts it. With --rm it is gone before you finish reading the output

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Forgetting the mount
The report renders and then vanishes




docker run --rm datasci350-project

[...]
Output created: report.html

Rendered report is in output/report.html

ls output
ls: output: No such file or directory
exit code: 1


The container said it succeeded. It did succeed
It wrote /project/output/report.html inside itself, --rm deleted the container, and the file went with it
Nothing on your laptop changed



The file really existed. Here it is, listed from inside the same container before it exited:


docker run --rm datasci350-project bash -c \
  "quarto render report.qmd >/dev/null 2>&1 \
   && mkdir -p output && cp report.html output/ \
   && ls -la output"

-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1313598 report.html


The same 1,313,598 bytes as the mounted run produced
This is the most common Docker mistake in the course, and the terminal gives you no warning at all


Success inside a container that no longer exists is worth nothing to you. Check ls output after every run, and check the timestamp on the file

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Change one line, rebuild
Layer caching on a real project




I changed the title in report.qmd and built again:


time docker build --progress=plain -t datasci350-project .

#4 transferring context: 4.74kB done
#5 [1/8] FROM docker.io/library/ubuntu:24.04
#5 DONE 0.0s
#6 [2/8] RUN apt-get update && apt-get install [...]
#6 CACHED
#7 [3/8] RUN ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture) [...]
#7 CACHED
#8 [6/8] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r [...]
#8 CACHED
#9 [4/8] RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv
#9 CACHED
#10 [5/8] COPY requirements.txt /project/requirements.txt
#10 CACHED
#11 [7/8] WORKDIR /project
#11 CACHED
#12 [8/8] COPY . /project
#12 DONE 0.1s

docker build [...]  0.837 total



Seven steps cached, one rebuilt, and the whole build finished in 0.837 seconds against 7 minutes 00.70 seconds cold
Only COPY . /project saw new input, because only report.qmd changed
requirements.txt was untouched, so the 89-second pip install above it stayed cached
BuildKit reorders independent steps, which is why #8 reports step [6/8]
Edit requirements.txt instead and the cache misses at step [5/8], so pip and everything below it run again


Rebuild after every edit. A second is cheap, and it keeps the image and your source in step


Try it yourself

text:
Try it yourself! 🧠
Five minutes



Warning: step 3 downloads about 11 MB of wheels and took 156 seconds on my wifi.

In your clone of the starter, add pandas==3.0.5 under duckdb==1.5.5 in requirements.txt
Run docker build -t datasci350-project .

What to look for:

Steps [1/8] to [4/8] stay CACHED: Ubuntu, apt, Quarto, and the empty virtual environment are reused
The miss lands at [5/8] COPY requirements.txt, because that file changed
Everything below the miss rebuilds, and [6/8] RUN pip install runs from nothing for 156 seconds
The second build rebuilds only COPY . /project, so it finishes in seconds

pip freeze inside the image goes from 54 packages to 55

ls data

(nothing)

docker build -t datasci350-project-nodata .
#13 DONE 0.2s

section: Failure two: a pin that does not exist
text:
Failure two: a pin that does not exist
pip fails, the build stops, nothing below it is cached




I changed polars==1.43.2 to polars==1.43.9 and built:


#10 [6/8] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r [...]
[...]
#10 3.611 ERROR: Could not find a version that
    satisfies the requirement polars==1.43.9
    (from versions: [...] 1.42.1, 1.43.2, 1.44.0)
#10 3.611 ERROR: No matching distribution found
    for polars==1.43.9

Dockerfile:85
--------------------
  84 |     COPY requirements.txt /project/requirements.txt
  85 | >>> RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /project/requirements.txt
--------------------
ERROR: failed to build: failed to solve: process
"/bin/bash -c pip install [...]" did not complete
successfully: exit code: 1



A BuildKit error has three useful parts: the step number [6/8] names the instruction, Dockerfile:85 with the >>> marker names the line, and the message above is pip’s own output
The image is never created, so docker images shows no new entry
Layers [1/8] to [5/8] stay cached, so fixing the pin costs you the pip step and nothing more
Check a version before you pin it:


pip index versions polars

polars (1.44.0)
Available versions: 1.44.0, 1.43.2, 1.42.1, [...]
  INSTALLED: 1.43.2


Lecture 23’s appendix listed No matching distribution found as an error you would meet. Here it is in a real build, with a line number attached

text:
Inspecting a container that misbehaves
docker run -it and what it tells you




Anything after the image name replaces the CMD, so this starts a shell instead of rendering:

docker run --rm -it datasci350-project bash

Then look around, the way you would on any Linux machine:


quarto --version
1.9.37

which python
/opt/venv/bin/python

python -c "import polars, duckdb, matplotlib; \
  print(polars.__version__, duckdb.__version__, \
        matplotlib.__version__)"
1.43.2 1.5.5 3.10.8

ls data/raw
life_expectancy.csv
life_expectancy_raw.json

pwd
/project

whoami
root



Seven answers to the seven questions you actually have when a render fails: which Quarto, which Python, which packages, is the data there, where am I, who am I
-i keeps standard input open and -t gives you a terminal. Together they make an interactive session
docker exec -it <container> bash does the same on a container that is already running
Anything you install in there disappears when the container exits. Fix requirements.txt and rebuild instead
docker logs <container> prints the output of a container you started without watching


This is the fastest way to settle an argument about whether a package is in the image. Ten seconds inside the container beats ten minutes of reading the Dockerfile

Cleaning up
Images are big, and Docker never deletes anything by itself



$ docker ps -a
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE         STATUS
5594bb583fbd   hello-world   Exited (0) 2 hours ago

$ docker system df
TYPE          TOTAL  ACTIVE  SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images        7      1       10.88GB   4.029GB (37%)
Containers    1      0       0B        0B
Build Cache   37     0       3.046GB   1.403GB

$ docker rm youthful_vaughan
$ docker rmi datasci350-project-nodata
[...]
$ docker system prune
[...]
Total reclaimed space: 1.931GB

$ docker system df
Images        4      0       3.217GB   1.97GB (61%)
Containers    0      0       0B        0B
Build Cache   8      0       1.643GB   0B

One project image is 1.64GB on disk here. Three experiments and a couple of failed builds and you are into double figures










Command
What it removes




docker ps -a
Nothing, it lists containers including exited ones


docker rm <id>
One stopped container


docker rmi <image>
One image


docker system df
Nothing, it reports what is using space


docker system prune
Stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, build cache


docker system prune -a
All of the above plus every image not in use





A dangling image is one with no tag, usually left behind when you rebuilt a tag onto a new image
--rm on docker run is what stops the container list growing in the first place


docker system prune -a deletes every image no running container is using, including the one you spent seven minutes building. Read the prompt before you type y

Docker Compose
The same build and run, written down once




Typing docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/output:/project/output" datasci350-project twenty times is how typos happen:


services:
  report:
    build: .
    image: datasci350-project
    volumes:
      - ./output:/project/output


Save it as compose.yaml next to your Dockerfile:

docker compose up --build
docker compose down

Compose reads the relative path ./output for you, so $(pwd) never appears
Compose exists for multi-container work: a database, an API, and a notebook talking to each other. One service is the small end of it

What we learned today
One file, fourteen instructions, one test




The project starter gives you a working pipeline: a pull script, a committed snapshot, a report, and a Dockerfile

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 02: When something goes wrong
Seven errors from this lecture’s build



FileNotFoundError: [...] life_expectancy.csv
The snapshot never reached the repository. Run git add data/raw/, commit, and check with git ls-files data/raw.
No matching distribution found for polars==1.43.9
That version does not exist on PyPI. Run pip index versions polars and pin one it lists.
ls: output: No such file or directory
You ran the container without -v. Add -v "$(pwd)/output:/project/output", or ${PWD} in PowerShell.
error: externally-managed-environment
You ran pip install against Ubuntu’s own Python. Create a virtual environment and put /opt/venv/bin first in PATH.

failed to read dockerfile: open Dockerfile
You are in the wrong folder. The . in docker build -t name . is where Docker looks, so cd into the folder with the Dockerfile.
NoSuchKernel: No such kernel named python3
ipykernel is missing from requirements.txt, so Quarto cannot start a kernel. Put ipykernel==7.2.0 back and rebuild.
toomanyrequests: pull rate limit
Docker Hub allows 100 anonymous pulls per hour from one address. Run docker login and build again.

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Appendix 03: The complete Dockerfile
As shipped in the starter



# 1. Base image
# FROM chooses the starting point: Ubuntu 24.04,
# the system you saw in the containers lecture.
# We pin the tag to "24.04" rather than "latest".
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# 2. Build-time settings
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]

# 3. System packages
# We do not pin apt versions here. Ubuntu replaces
# a version whenever it ships a security fix, and a
# pin that no longer exists stops the build. The
# base image tag and requirements.txt carry the pins.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates \
    wget \
    git \
    python3.12 \
    python3.12-venv \
    python3-pip && \
    apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# 4. Quarto
ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.37
RUN ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture) && \
    wget -q "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends "./quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    rm "quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${ARCH}.deb" && \
    apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# 5. Python environment
# Ubuntu protects its own Python installation, so
# we create a virtual environment at /opt/venv and
# install our packages there.
RUN python3 -m venv /opt/venv

# PATH tells the shell where to look for programs.
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

# We copy requirements.txt on its own, before the
# rest of the project. Docker caches each layer.
COPY requirements.txt /project/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /project/requirements.txt

# 6. Project files
# WORKDIR sets the folder that later instructions
# run inside.
WORKDIR /project

# Copy everything else from your repository into
# the image, including report.qmd and the saved
# data snapshot in data/raw/.
# The .dockerignore file next to this one lists
# what stays out.
COPY . /project

# 7. Default command
# We render first and copy afterwards. Quarto
# clears its output folder before writing, and it
# cannot clear a folder Docker mounted from outside.
# QUARTO_PYTHON points Quarto at the venv's Python.
ENV QUARTO_PYTHON=/opt/venv/bin/python
CMD ["bash", "-c", "quarto render report.qmd && mkdir -p output && cp -a report.html output/ && echo 'Rendered report is in output/report.html'"]

The starter is at commit 7d79f5b, plus the .dockerignore and comment fix made for this lecture
Comments are trimmed here. The file in your clone explains every line

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Serial and parallel work
Where lecture 21 started




Serial: each line finishes before the next one starts
Parallel: independent tasks run at the same time on several cores
map applies one function to every element of a list

Every parallel tool copies that shape

A problem is embarrassingly parallel when the tasks share no state and need no result from each other
Our calculation() on ten million random numbers qualified

A loop carrying a running total does not

Four parallel calls never reached a full 4× saving: starting workers and moving results back costs time



def bar(x):
    return x * x

foo = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

list(map(bar, foo))
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]


Before parallelising anything:

Are the tasks independent?
Is each one heavy enough to pay for starting a worker?

If either answer is no, the cores will not help you

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing

joblib and concurrent.futures
When to reach for each one




joblib turns a loop into parallel work in two lines

n_jobs=-1 uses every core



from joblib import Parallel, delayed

results = Parallel(n_jobs=6)(
    delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo
)


sklearn calls joblib internally whenever you set n_jobs=-1
concurrent.futures ships with Python, so it works where you cannot install anything



The choice comes from why the task is slow:










Your task
Tool
Why




Number crunching
ProcessPoolExecutor
The processor is busy

ThreadPoolExecutor
The processor is idle, waiting


sklearn, numeric loops
joblib
Calls processes for you


Bigger than RAM
Dask
Chunks the data itself





CPU-bound work needs more processors
I/O-bound work needs cheap threads that wait
Both executors copy the map interface: a function and an iterable

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Big O
How the runtime grows with the input




Big O describes how the runtime grows as the input grows
O(1) constant, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic: doubling the input costs nothing, twice as much, or four times as much
With p cores, an O(n) problem becomes O(n/p + overhead)
Parallelism divides the constant in front of the class, and never the class itself
pairwise_sum on 1,000 elements is a million operations, and 10 billion at 100,000

No core count rescues that

An O(n log n) algorithm beats a parallelised O(n²) one on any interesting input



# O(n^2): every pair of elements
def pairwise_sum(data):
    n = len(data)
    results = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            results.append(data[i] + data[j])
    return results


Poor candidates for parallelism:

Steps that depend on the previous result
Algorithms with shared state
Work limited by memory rather than by the CPU

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Amdahl’s law
The serial share caps your speed-up




Every program has a serial share: the setup, the merging of the results, and any step that waits for the one before it
The formula is \(\text{speedup} = \dfrac{1}{s + \dfrac{p}{N}}\), with \(s\) the serial fraction, \(p = 1 - s\) the parallel fraction, and \(N\) the number of cores
A program that is 90% parallel, on 8 cores:


s = 0.1        p = 0.9        N = 8

1 / (0.1 + 0.9/8)
  = 1 / (0.1 + 0.1125)
  = 1 / 0.2125
  = 4.7x



Eight cores give 4.7×: half the hardware does nothing for you
Push \(N\) to infinity and the ceiling is \(1/s\), which is 10× here
A 50% serial program never passes 2×, however large the cluster
Measure before you scale: %timeit and cProfile tell you what \(s\) actually is
Expect this arithmetic in the quiz

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
The GIL
Why one thread runs Python at a time




CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock: one thread runs Python code at a time, however many cores you own
Threads still help while your code waits, because the lock is released during a download or a disk read
Threads do nothing while your code computes, because the lock keeps the others idle
CPU-bound work needs processes, each one a separate Python with its own lock
NumPy, Polars and DuckDB release the GIL while their C and Rust code runs, so they use every core with no processes to manage
A free-threaded build is official since Python 3.14, and it is not the default






Task
Use




Number crunching
Processes


Downloading many URLs
Threads


NumPy, Polars, DuckDB
Either or neither


sklearn with n_jobs=-1
Processes, via joblib





The quiz will ask you to pick one. Start from the lock: it is released while Python waits and held while Python computes

title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing
text:
Dask
Lazy evaluation, and when a cluster is worth it




Dask gives you lazy versions of tools you already use: Array for NumPy, DataFrame for pandas, delayed for your own functions, Distributed for a cluster
Lazy means nothing runs until .compute(), and until then you are building a task graph
The graph lets Dask optimise the plan and keep memory down before any work starts
.persist() computes a result once and holds it in RAM

Use it on a small aggregate, never on the raw frame

joblib parallelises your functions and leaves the data alone
Dask chunks the data itself, so a frame can be larger than your RAM
The dashboard at localhost:8787 shows the task stream live, and white space in a row means an idle worker



A cluster pays for itself when the data does not fit on the machine, or when the graph has real dependencies between tasks
When the data fits in memory it costs you: building the graph and moving chunks can make Dask slower than pandas
Parquet cut our January 2000 data from 182 MB to 86 MB and made the group-by much faster
